#5758. BCBSMA, Medzown team up to match members with clinical trials

BCBSMA, Medzown team up to match members with clinical trials" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts is teaming up with precision medicine company Medzown to make it easier for members with complex conditions to participate in clinical trials.

In the partnership, Medzown's tech stack will identify the members that are most likely to benefit from a novel therapy for their condition, and then match them with potential clinical trials. The company will then deploy a team of scientists, clinical trial experts and care navigators to work alongside the patient and their care team through the process.

Jennifer Levin Carter, M.D., the CEO of Medzown, told Fierce Healthcare that there's no shortage of new drugs and therapies coming through the pipeline for complex diseases like cancer, but access is a significant challenge.

"The next frontier for precision medicine is making sure that the right patient can actually get access," Carter said.

BCBSMA will notify members of their eligibility for the program, and participation is voluntary. The program is offered at no additional cost for members.

Karl Laskowski, M.D., vice president for clinical programs and strategy at BCBSMA, said in an interview that complex diseases like cancer are often scary and difficult for patients to navigate, and clinical trials offer access to therapies or care they "wouldn’t have otherwise at their disposal."

"It is not always clear what to do, and there’s a lot coming at you," he said. "We want to show up as a trusted ally, making sure that we are filling a need there for people to get advice, taking advantage of whatever may be the most appropriate."

The insurer said that the partnership with Medzown builds on its existing work to manage complex diseases. For example, in June, BCBSMA entered a value-based care contract with Thyme Care, offering its services as an extension of the patient's current care team.

It's BCBSMA's first specialty-specific value-based care relationship, the insurer said.

Laskowski said that it's early days for the partnership with Medzown, but the team is gathering feedback on what's working and what's not to continue improving and building on this foundation.

Carter echoed the sentiment, saying that while there's likely "tremendous opportunity" to grow from here, the focus is on making sure the current program is functioning at the highest level for the members it serves.

She added that the Medzown team believes that a precision medicine data layer will be critical to healthcare more broadly as the treatment for complex disease becomes more and more personal.

"Treatment of cancer has totally changed for many cancer types," she said. "It has turned into a disease that can be managed on a long-term and chronic basis."

"We need to be able to integrate that ... so that these great and fabulous new esoteric therapies get into the continuum of care," Carter said.

#5757. The Harley-Davidson Sprint 440 Is Exactly What Harley Needs

It's finally happening: Harley-Davidson is bringing a proper Harley-looking beginner bike to the United States. Not some weird half-baked attempt like the Street line, but a proper Harley-styled cruiser that just happens to be built around a smaller, beginner-friendly engine. The new bike is called the Sprint 440, it's debuting at EICMA, and I couldn't be more excited for it.

I've long said that Harley needs a proper beginner bike, a way into the brand that capitalizes on what Milwaukee does well — vintage, call it "authentic" styling — without the company's usual high prices and general skull-themed accessorizing. The Sprint 440 appears to be just that: A practical single cylinder, a Sportster-esque sloped tank, and a price that lets beginners actually cross-shop Harley with Kawasaki and Triumph. While we don't know the firm U.S. price yet, we know the bike goes for just $8,500 Canadian up north — the equivalent of just over $6,000 here.

The Sprint looks leagues better than the Nightster it displaces as Harley's cheapest bike, with styling that better hides the brake lines, wires, and radiators a modern motorcycle requires. The Sprint could be mistaken for an Iron 883 by those who don't know the ins and outs of both bikes, though it does need some indicators of its foreign coproduction — the bike is a collaboration with India's Hero MotoCorp, according to RideApart, and its chain drive demonstrates that things aren't all Harley here. Still, it's a Milwaukee bike in the ways that really matter: Despite the foreign assistance, Harley says the bike will undergo final production in Pennsylvania.

Harley hasn't yet released all the specs for the U.S. model of the Sprint, but we know the international model has a 26.4-inch seat height (though Harley specifies that's "laden") and a 412-pound weight. Horsepower is low, at just 27, though it makes a full 28 pound-feet of torque. Those numbers aren't incredibly impressive, but if you're a new rider into the looks of a classic Harley you probably won't mind — you'll just appreciate a lighter, cheaper way to get the bike you want. That kind of accessibility is what Harley has been lacking for years, and I truly hope the Sprint 440 helps the brand get some new buyers in.

#5756. Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles

Most primates have relatively large brains covered in distinctive folds and grooves. However, common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) are an unusual exception. These small monkeys have brains that are almost entirely smooth, with very little folding. Scientists at the German Primate Center (DPZ), the Leibniz Institute for Primate Research in Göttingen, have now identified several cellular processes that help explain this difference.

Using miniature brain structures known as organoids, the researchers discovered that certain neural progenitor cells, which produce neurons, develop differently in marmosets than in humans. These differences involve the cells' structure, the speed at which they divide, and the timing of their development. Together, these changes reduce the number of neurons produced, contributing to the smaller size and smoother surface of the marmoset brain. Published in Science Advances, the findings provide new insights into primate brain evolution and could eventually improve our understanding of human brain development disorders.

Why Some Primate Brains Are Smooth Instead of Folded

Brain size and the extent of surface folding are important features that distinguish different primate species. The human brain, for example, has a highly folded surface resembling the ridges and grooves of a walnut. This arrangement greatly expands the brain's surface area, creating room for billions of neurons that support complex thinking and other advanced mental abilities.

Scientists believe that the common ancestor of modern primates already possessed a moderately sized brain with at least some folding. Yet not all primates living today retain these characteristics.

Common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus), small monkeys native to South America that are becoming increasingly important in biomedical research, have brains with almost no visible folds. Researchers at the German Primate Center set out to determine why their brains develop so differently from those of humans and other primates.

"We wanted to understand which changes at the cellular level cause the marmoset brain to grow less and form fewer folds," explains Lidiia Tynianskaia, one of the study's two first authors and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution at the DPZ. "At the beginning of development, the common marmoset brain exhibits the typical structure and composition of a large, folded primate brain. As development progresses, processes must therefore occur that effectively slow down the production of nerve cells."

Scientists Discover What Slows Brain Growth

To investigate these developmental differences, the team compared brain organoids grown from human and common marmoset cells. Their attention centered on neural progenitor cells, the cells responsible for generating neurons during brain development.

These progenitor cells play a major role in determining the eventual size and shape of the brain. The more neurons they produce, the greater the potential for the cerebral cortex to expand and develop folds.

The researchers found that the marmoset's smaller, smoother cerebral cortex is not the result of a single developmental change. Instead, several differences involving distinct types of progenitor cells work together to limit neuron production and brain folding.

"Our investigations have shown that certain progenitor cells in the common marmoset divide significantly more slowly than in humans," explains César Mateo Bastidas Betancourt, also a first author of the study and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group. "Other progenitor cells have a simpler structure than their human counterparts, with fewer processes, and are therefore less proliferative. Both of these factors ultimately result in fewer nerve cells, which contributes to a smaller size and less folding of the cerebral cortex in marmosets."

The scientists also identified important differences in when certain progenitor cell characteristics and behaviors emerge during development. Compared with humans, marmosets have a shorter overall period during which these cells can multiply rapidly.

Together, the slower rate of cell division, simpler cell structures, and shorter window for rapid growth help explain why the marmoset brain produces fewer neurons and develops far fewer folds.

Miniature Brains Reveal Important Developmental Clues

Much of the research relied on brain organoids, small, three-dimensional structures grown from cells that reproduce important features of early brain development. These miniature models allowed scientists to investigate developmental changes across multiple samples and compare the timing of key processes.

"The study combines the advantages of in vivo and in vitro methods," says Michael Heide, head of the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution. "Organoids are well-suited for obtaining statistically robust results because such sample sizes are not feasible in primates. We subsequently repeated some key experiments in fetal brain tissue to confirm the results from the organoids."

One particularly important finding involved the relationship between development in organoids and development in actual marmoset brains. The researchers determined that a marmoset brain organoid grown for 50 days closely matches the developmental stage of a natural marmoset brain at day 90.

Establishing this relationship was essential because brain organoids and actual brains do not necessarily develop at the same rate. By identifying corresponding developmental stages, the scientists could make meaningful comparisons and interpret their experimental findings more reliably.

What Smooth Monkey Brains Reveal About Human Brain Evolution

The findings help explain how relatively small differences in the behavior and developmental timing of brain-building cells can contribute to major differences in brain size and folding among primates.

They also offer a potential explanation for how the wide variety of primate brain shapes and sizes emerged over evolutionary time, including why some species developed relatively smooth brains while others possess much larger, heavily folded ones.

Beyond their evolutionary significance, these discoveries provide a foundation for investigating how the human brain develops and what happens when those processes are disrupted. A better understanding of the cellular mechanisms that control neuron production and brain growth could ultimately help researchers study developmental disorders affecting the human brain.

#5755. Tenet Healthcare sails past Q3 earnings estimates, boosts 2026 guidance

Tenet Healthcare sails past Q3 earnings estimates, boosts 2026 guidance" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Strong performance across its hospital and ambulatory businesses during the third quarter led Tenet Healthcare to raise its 2026 earnings guidance by 4%, with executives asserting that the core strength of operations will yield continued earnings growth in 2027 despite policy headwinds.

The for-profit this week reported $5.63 billion in net operating revenues for the quarter, not counting $646 million in contract termination revenue tied to its divorce with CommonSpirit Health that was recognized during the quarter. The tally was 6.5% above the same period last year and above the $5.47 billion consensus estimate, per Zacks Investment Research.

The bigger standouts were its $6.64 adjusted earnings per share, well above the prior year’s $3.70 earnings per share and more than 40% above the consensus estimate of $4.60 per share. Further, executives highlighted third-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $1.36 billion (about 16% above the street, per Stephens), about 10% year-over-year growth when excluding $147 million in one-time items stemming from the shifting timing of its CommonSpirit contract winddown.

Based on those results, the health system boosted 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance by $195 million, building on the prior increase issued during the summer. CEO Saum Sutaria, M.D., told analysts during a Thursday morning call that the change “is supported by our continued expectations for strong fundamental performance as well as the one-time items in the back half of the year. Notably, over 40% of our total guidance increase for this year is from fundamental outperformance.”

For the quarter, executives generally described rising hospital activity and continued expense reductions that outpaced industry-wide weak surgical volumes and payer mix challenges.

Specifically, same-hospital admissions rose 2.8% year over year, adjusted admissions rose 3.2% and hospital surgeries dipped 1.1%. Net hospital revenues rose 6.1% year over year while revenue per adjusted admission rose a narrower 0.2%, as “continued pricing strength” and volumes outpaced 18% declines in exchange admissions and revenues, executives said.

Adjusted EBITDA for the hospitals business grew from last year’s $607 million to $818 million (including the $147 million one-time items). The segment also recognized $32 million more in favorable pre-tax impact tied to supplemental Medicaid payments compared to the prior year, or $356 million in total.

In Tenet’s high-margin ambulatory segment, same-facility net patient service revenues rose 4.5% year over year despite a 1.5% drop in same-facility cases. Same-facility net revenue per case rose 6.1%, which executives said reflects the company’s ongoing strategic push to capture high-acuity patients. Adjusted EBITDA rose 9.1% year over year to $537 million.

On surgical numbers, which have been a sore spot for systems over the last few months, Sutaria said the company was pleased that both sides of the business were performing “generally consistent or better than we’re seeing in the general industry. … I would not say this is a gangbusters surgical environment right now.”

The ambulatory surgery market in particular has been heating up as health systems look to flesh out their networks and meet the calls for care in lower-cost settings. Sutaria, in response to an analyst question, acknowledged this week’s news that Bon Secours Mercy Health would be acquiring Surgery Partners in a $5.7 billion deal. Taken alongside the summer’s $3.9 billion AmSurg close by Ascension, he said that Tenet’s platform remains the standout for differentiated earnings growth. What’s more, the “attractive valuation of our equity, relative to what are some reasonable valuations of … ASC-hospital combination platforms” gives the company additional reason to repurchase its shares, he said.

“Look, in terms of the two recent ASC acquisitions, you know, I personally extended my congratulations to both new owners,” he said. This is an important part of the market and we have a lot of work to do together from an advocacy perspective in order to support and build the growing interest in ambulatory surgery, maintain high quality and safety, and also ensure that regulators understand the benefits that this portion of the surgical sector is providing to the cost of healthcare going forward. And so I look forward to those collaborations with those leaders.”

On concerns of dealmaking competition, Sutaria noted that the company was “very successful” in new ASC acquisitions during the quarter and that “the vast majority of which were not competitive processes, but came exclusively to [us] in those processes.”

As for next year, executives said Tenet is expected to grow its overall EBITDA. That’s after excluding the impacts of the CommonSpirit contract termination, and taking into account “the current known regulatory frameworks” such as those outlining Medicaid work requirements and supplemental payments.

Tenet’s stock was trading about 1% below the day’s open as of early afternoon. Its report comes after other large for-profits like HCA Healthcare and Universal Health Services outlined persistent payer mix and surgery concerns as well as tepid early guidance for 2027.

#5754. Buy A New Mazda Miata Today, You Will Not Regret Buying A Mazda Miata

Sometimes you order something online, only for it to arrive in a different size and color than you were expecting. The Mazda MX-5 Miata is not one of those things. It will never disappoint you, and I guarantee you won't regret buying one. So do it. Buy a new Mazda Miata. Come on, what are you waiting for? A sign? This is your sign. I am the prophet. The car gods have sent me to preach their message of salvation, and today I speak unto you, "Go buy a Mazda Miata. You will not regret buying a Mazda Miata."

Now, $32,640 is a lot of money, at least if you're spending it. It probably feels like a lot less if it's your annual income. But even if you make $326,400 a year, it's still not a sum many people will spend on a whim. Divide that MSRP by 60, though, and you get a much more manageable $544. A lot of people have room in their budget to spend $544 if they get creative with it. And if you're one of those people, the best thing you could do with that money would be to spend it on a new Mazda Miata.

Typically, you'll hear that a new car can only fix the problems in your life that your current car is causing. A new truck, for example, can't fix the fact that women find your personality off-putting and weird. Anyone who tells you that is probably right, but they're also wrong. Because while that's true for other cars, there's no problem in your life that a Mazda Miata can't fix.

Do you wish you had more friends? Buy a Miata, and you'll instantly be friends with every Miata owner and car enthusiast that you meet. Do you like talking to old people? Good. Because you're friends with all of them now, and I'm sorry, but they're all yappers. Everywhere you go, you'll find a community of Miata lovers, and because of that, you'll never be lonely again. Because you have a Miata, and no one can possibly be lonely as long as they own a Miata.

Are you trying to make yourself more attractive? I hear tall people are more attractive. And while doing something about your height is incredibly expensive and involves a long recovery, you can easily make your car shorter. By buying a Mazda Miata. How can you possibly look short if you're taller than your car? That's why everyone who drives an Escalade, Tahoe, or Suburban looks so short. They aren't taller than their cars, and it throws off the perspective.

Have other problems? Well, a Mazda Miata once treated my sciatica. And my brother once told me that after the first time he drove a Miata, his IBS was cured. #5753. Washington State Resident Dies From Bird Flu Following Exposure to Infected Cattle

— Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since 2024

A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such U.S. death in a year.

The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized. The person died Sunday, county health officials said.

Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5.

Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The CDC said the person was infected with H5N1.

County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds recently have tested positive for H5N1.

They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms.

The H5N1 bird flu has been spreading widely among wild birds, poultry, cows, and other animals for several years. Health concerns escalated in early 2024 when infections spread among U.S. livestock. Its presence in the environment increases the chances that people will be exposed, and potentially catch it, officials have said.

More than 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since the beginning of 2024, according to the CDC. But there is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says.

The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday.

Officials continue to urge people who have contact with sick or dead birds to take precautions, including wearing respiratory and eye protection and gloves when handling poultry. People who work on farms are considered to be at higher risk.

#5752. Community Health Systems logs $86M net loss in Q3, hopes for return of 'pent-up' electives in 2027

Community Health Systems logs $86M net loss in Q3, hopes for return of 'pent-up' electives in 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A “challenging macro environment” serving up more uninsured patients and fewer commercial elective procedures dragged Community Health Systems below internal and analyst operating forecasts for the third quarter.

The 59-hospital system reported $2.76 billion in third-quarter net operating revenue, down about 10.7% year over year due to several divestments but up 3.8% on a same-store basis. Net loss was $86 million, -$0.63 per diluted share or -$0.48 after adjustment, compared to the prior year’s $1.27 per share net income.

The consensus estimates for revenue and earnings were $2.78 billion and -$0.22 per diluted share, per Zach’s Investment Research. The company’s shares were trading over 10% below the open late Thursday afternoon.

“While overall financial results fell below our internal forecast, due to the same factors that many peers are experiencing—namely elevated uninsured volumes and temporary softness in commercial elective procedures—we delivered sequential volume gains and solid cash flow performance,” CEO Kevin Hammons summarized Thursday morning on the company’s earnings call. “Importantly, our leading indicators clearly demonstrate that care is being deferred rather than lost to competitors.”

CHS has reduced its 2026 guidance ranges for net operating revenues, adjusted EBITDA and cash ranges.

Same-store admissions rose 2.2% while adjusted admissions increased 3.6% year over year. However, about half of the adjusted admissions growth was among uninsured patients, Chief Financial Officer Jason Johnson explained, and a 2% overall increase in same-store surgeries masked low numbers for commercial electives. These factors held same-store net revenue per adjusted admission to just 0.2% year-over-year growth.

Executives, in response to analyst questions, noted that the 2% increase is a clear improvement from recent quarters’ declines.

“We saw more cardiac procedures and more GI procedures this quarter,” Hammons explained. “The cardiac procedures, though, … are low margin because of the high cost of the devices. What we were short on were the elective orthopedic and elective general surgery-type procedures that are higher-margin business, and those are more elective type procedures. […] Again, kind of fits back into the story of we believe this is a patient decision around care, and being influenced by financial decisions.”

In the meantime, Hammons said the company is “proactively managing our cost structure,” yielding more than $100 million in projected annual savings so far “without compromising our clinical capacity or operational readiness for tomorrow” when those electives return.

Looking to the tea leaves in 2027, executives suggested there would be a “modest” headwind from Medicaid work requirements. While more than half of the company’s Medicaid volumes are in expansion states, “we think it’s likely that the very large majority will qualify for continued coverage under the various exemptions like age, caregiver status or medical frailty, but we really just don’t know exactly what the impact will be until the data starts coming in,” Johnson said during the call.

Exchange volume reductions due to coverage drop-offs could see “some potential future degradation” based on how open enrollment goes, he said, although “we think there will be a modest headwind there.” Provider tax cuts will also likely bring another “modest” hit, while medical specialty fees expected to grow “well above inflation” are “the big question mark on cost,” Johnson added.

On the other hand, executives counted payment rate updates, investments in outpatient and ambulatory locations, expense management and $25 million to $30 million in year-one funds from the Rural Health Transformation Program as positive factors for 2027 earnings.

Further, they suggested that this year’s “uncharacteristic” dearth in elective procedures could come to an end as cost-conscious patients—who are still captured in CHS’ care networks—eventually book their deferred care.

“There’s pent-up demand,” Hammons said. “Ultimately, we think that it comes back into the system because when you need a joint replacement, it’s not going to heal on its own.”

“Our initial expectations [were that when] we got into the back half of this year, we would see that seasonality growth. We did not see as much of that in the third quarter as we had previously expected,” he explained. “As you get to October, if people have not met their co-pay and deductible, it’s likely they could push that off until next year, get their procedures in the first half of the year and have a longer period of time to have other medical procedures done without having to pay a co-pay and deductible again. So we’ve adjusted our guidance accordingly to reflect our outlook on that.”

CHS is hardly alone in navigating surgery and payer mix challenges. Fellow for-profits HCA Healthcare, Universal Health Services and Tenet Healthcare each described varying levels of impact during earnings calls held this week. Each held off from detailing concrete estimates for the coming year, noting a need to monitor year-end trends and the exchanges’ open enrollment period, but acknowledged that Medicaid coverage will likely continue to be a sore spot.

#5751. Oxford scientists discover how viruses build themselves without a blueprint

Researchers at the University of Oxford have observed virus-like particles assembling themselves one molecule at a time, uncovering the surprisingly simple rules that allow complex biological structures to form with remarkable reliability. The findings, published in Nature, offer a detailed look at a process that scientists have struggled to observe directly for decades.

Understanding how viruses construct their protective protein shells, and how that construction might be interrupted, could lead to new antiviral drugs, improved vaccines, and other medical treatments. The discovery helps explain how individual proteins consistently organize themselves into the correct structures despite having thousands of possible ways to connect.

The researchers found that viral assembly resembles navigating a complicated maze, where only certain paths lead to lasting progress. At first, protein components form weak connections that can easily break apart if the arrangement is unsuccessful. This flexibility allows the molecules to keep trying different combinations until they form particular closed structures. Once multiple connections hold these structures together, they become far more stable.

These stable arrangements serve as molecular checkpoints, narrowing the enormous number of possible assembly routes into a much smaller set of successful pathways. One especially important milestone occurs when five larger protein building blocks connect to form a closed pentagonal ring. This is the first highly stable structure in the assembly process. Once it forms, each subsequent stable stage requires fewer additional building blocks, allowing the particle to grow more quickly.

Co-lead author Dr. Roi Asor (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, University of Oxford) explained: "A virus has to solve an extraordinary construction problem. Its components somehow have to find the right arrangement among a huge number of possibilities, without a blueprint or machinery directing the process. We can now watch what happens molecule by molecule and see the physical rules that make it possible."

Watching Virus Particles Assemble Molecule by Molecule

Viruses store and protect their genetic material within organized protein shells known as capsids. Depending on the virus, these shells may consist of tens or even thousands of individual protein components. Remarkably, in many cases, the proteins can arrange themselves into the correct structure without any external machinery directing their assembly.

Although scientists have investigated viral self-assembly for decades, capturing the process as it unfolds has been a major challenge. Many of the intermediate structures exist only briefly and appear in very small quantities. As a result, traditional methods have generally allowed researchers to examine the starting materials and finished particles without clearly showing how one transforms into the other.

To overcome this limitation, the Oxford researchers studied an engineered virus-like particle composed of 60 protein units. They used mass photometry, a technique developed at Oxford that determines the mass of individual molecules by measuring the light they scatter. By combining this technology with a new approach for keeping individual molecules confined and continuously observable, the team could repeatedly measure the mass of a growing particle as additional proteins attached.

This approach allowed the scientists to follow the construction process as it happened, effectively tracking the addition of individual molecular building blocks over time.

Co-first author PhD student Dan Loewenthal (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, University of Oxford) said: "This method lets us study the assembly process directly, we just take a video!"

Co-lead author Professor Philipp Kukura (Department of Chemistry and Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, Oxford University) said: "Until now, much of our understanding of how these structures assemble has had to be reconstructed from snapshots or theoretical models. Being able to both quantify the underlying interactions and follow one particle as it grows changes that. We can see the important intermediate structures appear and deduce a detailed model of the construction process."

The Surprising Trick That Makes Viral Assembly Work

The results help explain how a process involving an overwhelming number of possible molecular arrangements can consistently produce the correct structure. Rather than exploring every possible route, the proteins progress through a relatively small number of stable intermediate stages that guide assembly toward completion.

The findings also clarify why the earliest stage of construction, called nucleation, is particularly difficult and why growth becomes substantially faster after the first stable structure appears.

A key part of this efficiency comes from the ability of protein building blocks to make mistakes without permanently disrupting the process. Weak initial connections allow incorrect combinations to separate, giving the proteins another opportunity to find a better arrangement. When enough components eventually connect in the correct closed configuration, the resulting structure becomes stable enough to support further growth.

Dr. Asor added: "The weak interactions give the system room to make mistakes. Most encounters don't have to be successful: the components can separate and try again. But once enough of them come together in the right closed arrangement, the structure becomes stable, and assembly can move forward. That combination of trial and error followed by locking in successful structures is what makes the process so reliable."

New Possibilities for Antiviral Drugs and Vaccines

By identifying the molecular interactions that control viral assembly, scientists may eventually be able to develop treatments that interfere with the construction of viral protein shells. The same insights could also support efforts to engineer virus-like particles for vaccines and other therapeutic applications.

Co-author Dr. Jack Tan (MRC Weatherall Institute of Molecular Medicine and CAMS-Oxford Institute) noted: "The ability to understand these processes at the molecular level could have important applications in vaccine development and antivirals that disrupt viral assembly."

The implications may extend far beyond viruses. Self-assembly is essential throughout biology, helping create everything from the internal skeletons of cells to specialized molecular compartments and large protein complexes.

By making it possible to observe these intricate construction processes one molecule at a time, the Oxford team's approach offers researchers a powerful new way to investigate how complex biological structures emerge from relatively simple interactions.

#5750. Turtle Wax Is Concerned About Your Love Life, And Claims Messy Cars Impact Dating

Dating today can be "a nightmare of confusion and poor outcomes," according to Psychology Today, but don't worry, Jalopnik and Turtle Wax are on the case. We've already checked in with readers to see which cars to avoid on a first date, along with which ones instantly tell you their owners have good taste. Now, thanks to a survey recently commissioned by the Turtle Wax team, we can go a little deeper: If you really want to make a good impression the next time you take someone out, first take the time to clean up your car.

The survey, conducted by Talker Research on behalf of Turtle Wax, looked at what people thought about potential partners' car-care routines. For instance, out of the 2,000 "actively dating Americans" questioned, 73% said the way people take care of their cars and the way they take care of themselves go hand in hand. Moreover, 67% of those surveyed responded that they can tell if people have messy personal lives by looking at how messy their vehicles are. Coming at it from the other angle, 65% of the survey respondents agreed that a clean, well-ordered vehicle is a sign someone has a clean, well-ordered life.

In fact, 25% of the folks surveyed said they've ended a date early because the driver's car was dirty. The real surprise is that that number wasn't any higher. After all, some of the disgusting items survey-takers had seen in cars included at least one box with a dead cat in it, live roaches and maggots, bottles of urine, moldy milk, and that all-time classic, used condoms.

Driving a messy car can affect more than just your chance for romance. Working our way from the outside in, one welcome benefit of a clean exterior is that it can improve your vehicle's fuel economy — if the car starts out dirty enough, it can see a fuel-efficiency gain approaching 10% once it's been cleaned. And every percentage point counts, given today's fuel prices.

Some road filth can actively damage your car as well. Tree sap and bird poop are prime examples: They can eat right through your vehicle's exterior finish if you don't clean them up promptly. It's a similar story with road salt and other corrosives, which can cause a car to rust if not regularly washed off. Either way, the result can be a cascade of problems. Keep the car, and you could face costly repairs. Try to sell it, and you're likely to get less for a cruddy-looking vehicle than for one that's been freshly detailed. Meanwhile, leaving grime and dust on your windows can turn into a major safety issue if they limit your visibility.

Getting into a car with a disgusting interior can open up its own set of issues. One of the worst is if you drop food or drinks in the cabin and simply leave the spill laying there. Then mold can start forming in your car. Oh, and remember the dead cat in a box mentioned above? Yeah, driving around with dead animals is another bad idea, since they can carry salmonella, hantavirus, e. coli, and more.

#5749. EV Owners Need To Lend Out Their Cars If They Want Regular People To Go Electric

Electric vehicles will probably never fully replace the internal combustion sports car, but mainstream daily drivers are living on borrowed time. It's not like anyone with no idea which wheels are powered or how many cylinders their car has cares about a missing exhaust note. But while EVs are taking off in the rest of the world, the U.S. lags behind, thanks in large part to pro-oil propaganda. People believe all sorts of myths about EVs, and I'm sorry, but short test drives won't fix it. Which means EV owners need to start acting like they have an obligation to lend friends and family their cars.

A few days in an EV won't change anyone's mind if their lifestyle doesn't match what EVs currently offer, and that's fine. But if they've been tricked by a bunch of pro-oil myths, you may find that a few days with your car is all it takes to convince them that EVs are the best thing ever. Because even an hour-long test drive doesn't show you the benefits of living with a gas station in your garage. It's the kind of thing that probably requires a three-day loan at a minimum, because they have to see how it fits into their regular lives.

Ideally, the automakers would take the lead here, but that's probably not happening anytime soon. I've discussed this idea with employees at several automakers, and so far, I don't think anyone wants to take on the cost and complexity of dealing with dealerships to make longer-term test drives happen. So without the automakers, it falls on the EV owners who want to see EVs become more popular. We need to be the ones pushing our cars on people like they're the supposed free samples that Deputy D. Diggity Dawg Dawson insisted drug dealers would force me to take.

At least anecdotally, I don't know of anything more powerful for changing minds about EVs than time spent with your butt in the seat. Most recently, a friend had to replace their beloved Mazda CX-5 after someone hit them; they asked me about EVs, and almost before I knew it, they were the proud new owners of a Hyundai Ioniq 5. So they were already open to a car that would save them money on gas, but even they quickly realized the things they were worried about weren't actually a big deal.

According to the friend, who I will call Bill, "driving them is super f—ing fun," and he did not think he "would enjoy trying to max out the mi/kWh using the regenerative braking... But [he does]." After only a few days of driving an EV, someone experiencing their first EV was already realizing how strong the oil propaganda is and how much better EVs are at things beyond saving money on gas.

An example of a borrowing experience changing minds is my brother — he borrowed my Fiat for a week while he was in the process of replacing his company truck. With three (soon to be four!) kids, he was never going to buy a two-door hatchback, but he loved being able to charge at home so much that he went out and bought a non-Fiat EV. All it took was a little time living with an electric car that he didn't even have any interest in owning, and it changed his mind about EV ownership before he'd even driven a competitive one.

I know it's scary letting other people borrow your car, and I certainly wouldn't want you handing the keys to someone you know is irresponsible. But without automaker or federal support, we're going to have to do this on our own, and the best way to get people to change their minds about EVs is to get some real time with the cars. And what better way to make that happen is there than trading cars with someone for a few days? Friends and family help each other out, after all.

If you lend your car to someone who decides they probably shouldn't buy an EV, that's fine. No harm, no foul. But just think how happy you'll be if a few days if your car convinces someone they've been wrong about EVs and should actually get one. It's pretty nice, I'm not going to lie, and definitely worth the risk of letting someone you know drive your car. They quite literally sell themselves.

#5748. Glioblastoma breakthrough reveals how brain cancer cells become more aggressive

Glioblastoma is among the most lethal forms of brain cancer, and scientists have uncovered a surprising factor that may help its cells become more invasive. The fluid surrounding the outer edges of these tumors is much thicker than the fluid near their centers, forcing cancer cells to encounter increasing resistance as they move into healthy brain tissue. Rather than simply slowing their movement, however, this environment appears to help the cells adapt in ways that make invasion easier.

To investigate this unexpected behavior, researchers created an innovative microfluidic chip that recreates the physical conditions encountered by glioblastoma cells. They found that spending extended periods in thick fluid caused the cells to become smaller, more flexible, and better able to squeeze through narrow openings. The discovery suggests that fluid viscosity does more than obstruct cancer cells. It can actively influence their behavior and potentially make them more aggressive.

How Thick Fluid Influences Brain Cancer Invasion

Cancer research has traditionally concentrated on chemical signals and the stiffness of the tissues surrounding tumors. Far less attention has been given to the viscosity of the fluid through which cancer cells travel.

In glioblastoma, this difference is particularly striking. Fluid at the tumor's advancing edge is approximately eight times more viscous than fluid in its dead tissue at the center. As cancer cells move outward, they must push through an increasingly resistant environment.

Studying this process has been difficult because conventional closed microfluidic devices cannot accurately reproduce these conditions. Their enclosed channels can limit access to oxygen and nutrients, while friction against the walls introduces additional forces that influence cell behavior. These limitations also make it challenging to observe how cancer cells respond to prolonged exposure to viscous fluid.

Researchers therefore needed a way to isolate the effects of fluid viscosity from other mechanical influences and determine whether extended exposure produces lasting changes in glioblastoma cells.

A New Device Reveals How Cancer Cells Adapt

Scientists from Chongqing General Hospital and Chongqing University in China developed a specialized open microfluidic platform to address these challenges. Their findings were published in Microsystems & Nanoengineering.

The device consists of a two-layer open microfluidic membrane equipped with a removable cap and an array of tiny pillars. This arrangement allows researchers to control precisely when cancer cells begin migrating while observing how their nuclei change shape as they move through confined spaces.

Unlike traditional enclosed systems, the platform also supports continuous cell culture for up to one month. This makes it possible to examine how prolonged mechanical stress changes the movement and invasive behavior of glioblastoma cells.

The researchers tested two human glioblastoma cell lines, U-251 and LN-229. Both were grown for a month in a thick fluid designed to reproduce conditions at the tumor's invasive outer edge (7.1 cP).

When the cells were subsequently examined using the chip, those that had adapted to the viscous environment traveled faster and covered greater distances than untreated control cells. This result was especially surprising because thicker fluid would ordinarily be expected to impede movement.

Brain Cancer Cells Become Smaller and More Flexible

Microscopic observations revealed how the adapted cells overcame this resistance. After prolonged exposure to the viscous fluid, they had become smaller and easier to deform, allowing them to maneuver through the narrow gaps between the device's microscopic pillars.

As the cells squeezed through these restricted passages, their nuclei underwent visible deformation. Researchers also observed an accumulation of YAP, a protein involved in sensing mechanical forces, inside the nuclei. This is a recognized sign that cells have activated pathways involved in responding to physical stress.

Although both glioblastoma cell lines developed similar changes in shape and movement, their underlying molecular responses were unexpectedly different.

U-251 cells underwent a form of mesenchymal-like reprogramming, activating genes associated with cancer invasion, including CD44, FN1, and MMP9. LN-229 cells, by contrast, became more flexible and mobile without showing substantial lasting changes in gene expression.

Further analysis using Western blotting showed that protein changes remained detectable even after cells were transferred back into fluid with normal viscosity. This indicated that at least some of the adaptations were persistent rather than simply short-lived responses to their surroundings.

Scientists Discover a Strange Kind of Cellular Memory

One of the most unexpected findings was that exposure to thick fluid appeared to leave a lasting imprint on glioblastoma cells.

The researchers had anticipated that viscosity would primarily function as a physical obstacle. Instead, their experiments showed that prolonged exposure could alter how cells behaved even after the original mechanical conditions were removed.

This phenomenon points to a form of mechanical memory, in which cells retain changes produced by earlier physical stress.

The open design of the new chip was essential for identifying this effect. By separating resistance from the fluid itself from the confinement imposed by channel walls, the researchers could investigate viscosity without the additional mechanical interference that complicates conventional experiments.

Observing changes in nuclear shape and migration patterns after weeks of exposure provided evidence that glioblastoma cells can adapt to their mechanical environment in lasting ways.

The contrasting molecular responses of the two cell lines were particularly revealing. Although both appeared to undergo similar physical transformations, only one showed extensive changes in its gene activity. This suggests that glioblastoma cells may acquire comparable invasive characteristics through different underlying biological processes.

A Potential New Approach to Studying Brain Cancer Treatments

Beyond uncovering an overlooked influence on glioblastoma invasion, the researchers believe their device could provide a valuable tool for investigating potential cancer therapies.

The open microfluidic platform fits into standard multi-well plates, allowing it to be incorporated into existing laboratory procedures for cell culture and imaging. Its accessible design also enables researchers to stain cells directly and observe them over long periods without the clogging problems that can occur in closed systems.

These features could make it useful for testing drugs that interfere with the cellular pathways responsible for detecting and responding to mechanical forces.

For glioblastoma, the results raise the possibility that highly viscous environments may favor cancer cells that are better adapted to invasion. Treatments targeting YAP signaling or the remodeling of the cytoskeleton, the internal framework that helps cells maintain and change their shape, could therefore be investigated under conditions that more closely resemble those inside tumors.

The technology may also prove useful for studying other cancers in which fluid viscosity varies across different regions. By examining how tumor cells respond to these mechanical conditions, researchers could gain a better understanding of why some cancers are particularly invasive and potentially identify patients whose tumors depend on mechanical adaptation to spread.

Although further research is needed to determine how these laboratory findings translate to tumors in patients, the discovery highlights an important and previously underexplored aspect of cancer biology: the physical environment surrounding tumor cells may actively shape their ability to invade healthy tissue.

#5747. Teladoc Health beats Q3 expectations as BetterHelp insurance growth accelerates

Teladoc Health beats Q3 expectations as BetterHelp insurance growth accelerates" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Teladoc Health raised its 2026 outlook after better-than-expected third-quarter results, as BetterHelp’s insurance pivot gained traction and Integrated Care profitability improved.

The virtual care company posted declining revenue but still beat Wall Street on both revenue and profit. Teladoc Health's Q3 beat drove shares up nearly 27% Thursday after the company reported Q3 earnings Wednesday after market close.

Teladoc Health faces near-term pressure as it transitions its virtual mental health business, BetterHelp, from a cash pay model to an in-network, insurance-covered model.

The company's consolidated revenue was $605.1 million, down 3.4% year-over-year but towards the high end of management's guidance range, as solid performance in the integrated care business and strong BetterHelp insurance growth was partially offset by ongoing headwinds in BetterHelp’s cash pay revenue, Chief Financial Officer Michael Grasher, who joined the company in August, told investors and analysts on the company's Q3 earnings call Wednesday. Teladoc's Q3 revenue exceeded the $588.4 million analyst consensus.

The company reported third-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $79.4 million, up roughly 14% year-over-year and compared to the $67.7 million consensus target. Teladoc reported a net loss of $26.9 million, or a loss per share of 15 cents, versus Street expectations for a loss of 22 cents per share.

The company generated $79 million in free cash flow in the third quarter, and it ended the quarter with $850 million in cash and cash equivalents.

Teladoc Health raised its full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance. The company now expects 2026 revenue of $2.39 billion to $2.44 billion, raising the midpoint of its full-year 2026 revenue outlook by $13 million, “driven largely by the updated BetterHelp outlook,” Grasher said.

The company expects adjusted EBITDA of $277 million to $303 million, up $3 million at the midpoint versus the prior range.

Teladoc Health is focused on expanding access to its direct-to-consumer virtual mental health services, BetterHelp, through insurance coverage while also growing its integrated care enterprise business.

"As we consider the market more broadly as a company, we continue to see opportunities for virtual care to play an increasing role in addressing key challenges in healthcare," Teladoc Health CEO Chuck Divita said during the call.

As a scaled virtual care company, Teladoc's technology and services help address rising healthcare costs, expand access, improve chronic disease and mental health care and ease pressure on providers and the broader healthcare system, Divita said.

The BetterHelp segment brought in $207 million in revenue, down 13% year-over-year. BetterHelp commercial insurance revenue exceeded expectations, coming in at $32.1 million, up from $3.7 million a year ago and beating management's forecast of $25 million to $31 million. BetterHelp cash-pay revenue declined 25% to $174 million in Q3, as fewer users paid out of pocket. But cash pay performance for BetterHelp was "better than anticipated," Divita said. The company continues to reduce advertising spend for the BetterHelp business while also "adapting its advertising and marketing approach to reflect insurance priorities," he noted.

BetterHelp's pivot to an in-network insurance model is gaining momentum with 27,000 covered sessions per week in Q3, an annualized run rate above $140 million and more than 11,000 credentialed therapists, Divita told analysts and investors. That compares to the $110 million annualized run rate from weekly sessions referenced in Teladoc's second-quarter earnings call.

In Q3, 36% of acquired U.S. users came from insurance, up about 8 percentage points from the second quarter, according to executives. The company added more than 3,000 therapists to the network during the quarter.

"We believe expanding insurance access can help create a more durable position for BetterHelp over time," Divita said.

The company expects continued growth in 2027 as it expands provider capacity, improves therapist engagement and grows utilization of BetterHelp’s services, Grasher said.

Teladoc is targeting a $200 million annualized BetterHelp insurance run rate by the end of 2027.

“While there is more work ahead, this was a solid quarter driven by execution, and continued progress across our key strategic priorities,” Grasher said.

Teladoc Health continues to invest in its core business, integrated care, which brought in $399 million in Q3 revenue, up 2% year-over-year, and adjusted EBITDA of $74.9 million, up 13% year-over-year. Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 18.8%, and Grasher noted on the call that the Q3 margin expansion occurred despite the ongoing mix shift toward visit-based arrangements.

The virtual company is focused on moving health plan and employer clients away from fragmented point solutions to its broader Teladoc One model. Teladoc One, unveiled in July, is designed to offer a more coordinated, personalized approach for members, while tying payment to clinical and financial outcomes, executives said. As part of the model, Teladoc Health care teams deliver and coordinate care across virtual settings and in partnership with a member's local providers.

The company has moved forward with initial launch partners for Teladoc One, and the platform will be more broadly available in 2027, executives said.

"We are encouraged by the level of client engagement and member feedback on Teladoc One at this point, reinforcing our view that clients are looking for solutions that can deliver a more connected experience, address more care needs, and demonstrate greater accountability for outcomes and impact," Divita said.

Outside the U.S. market, Teladoc Health developed a "hybrid care" model that combines its technology with virtual clinical services delivered into physical healthcare settings. The company sees opportunities to build out that model with U.S. hospitals and health systems. To support that strategy, Teladoc Health acquired Teledigm Health, a company that provides virtual clinical services to U.S. hospitals and health systems. Teledigm partners with hospitals and clinics to deliver remote acute, outpatient and specialty care.

Financial details of the Teledigm Health deal were not disclosed.

"We believe the market dynamics supporting the adoption of our hybrid care models in other countries are also increasingly prevalent with hospitals and health systems in the U.S., including healthcare workforce and capacity challenges, financial pressures and the need to improve access for underserved and rural communities. As a result, we see an opportunity to leverage our experience in hybrid care within the U.S. to support future growth," Divita said during the call.

"This is a company that we've worked with for a long time that's used our technology and really commercialized the services part of the equation using our technology. The tracks have been laid in terms of using our technology and support and use cases to those health systems. We think bringing that expertise we have in non-U.S. markets, which is considerable and has been a nice source of growth for us, bringing that expertise combined with our technology and telehealth services together, we can really go after that market opportunity in 2027," he told investors and analysts during a Q&A on the earnings call.

Teladoc also continues to invest in product innovation to support its integrated care business. The company expanded its Solo enterprise platform with two AI tools designed to add clinical capabilities without forcing hospitals to adopt more standalone technology. The two new capabilities—dubbed SoloVitals and SoloScribe—bring contact-free vital sign measurement and ambient clinical documentation directly into clinical workflows.

Wall Street analysts saw positive signs of progress in the turnaround of Teladoc's BetterHelp business in the latest quarter.

Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote that Teladoc's third-quarter results provided a positive update on the company’s ability to convert strong insurance demand into revenue.

"We continue to view BetterHelp’s transition toward greater in-network coverage as the key driver of business stabilization, particularly as insurance growth increasingly offsets cash-pay declines and added capacity of credentialed therapists enables the company to capture strong underlying demand," Daniels wrote in an analyst note.

"We are also encouraged by the company’s continued 2026 product introductions and launches across virtual care, including implementing Teladoc One with early launch partners and expanding hybrid care and AI-enabled solutions set to support continued growth in the Integrated Care segment," Daniels wrote.

However, ongoing weakness in BetterHelp’s cash-pay business "is likely to weigh on overall segment performance and temper the pace of the company’s broader turnaround," Daniels noted.

Teladoc remains in a transitional phase, Daniels noted, "navigating slower growth and a challenging end-market, with increased emphasis on profitability, product enhancements and capital deployment into new growth avenues."

#5746. Late-Stage Sickle Cell Disease Study Splits on Main Goals

— Mitapivat improved hemoglobin response, but no significant benefit for pain crises

The thalassemia drug mitapivat (Aqvesme) significantly improved hemoglobin response in patients with sickle cell disease but failed to top placebo when it came to reducing pain crises in a phase III trial that aims to support an expanded approval.

In the RISE UP trial, 41% of patients assigned to the oral pyruvate kinase activator had a hemoglobin response, as compared with 3% of placebo recipients (P<0.0001). But that didn't translate into a reduction in the annualized rate of sickle cell pain crises (2.6 for mitapivat vs 3.1 for placebo, P=0.1213), reported researchers led by Biree Andemariam, MD, of the New England Sickle Cell Institute at University of Connecticut Health in Farmington.

Beyond those two primary endpoints, treatment with mitapivat was associated with improved markers of hemolysis, reduced transfusion burden, and additional clinical benefits in the subset of patients with a hemoglobin response, but not with improvements in patient-reported fatigue, the study authors wrote in The Lancet.

These mitapivat data, which are currently under review with the FDA, arrive amid turbulence in the drug market for sickle cell disease. Crizanlizumab (Adakveo), approved in 2019, lost its marketing authorization in Europe after randomized trial data showed the drug failed to top placebo when it came to vaso-occlusive crises, though it's still available in the U.S.

And voxelotor (Oxbryta), which was granted accelerated approval, also in 2019, was pulled from global markets after trial data turned up an imbalance in deaths and acute vaso-occlusive crises for patients on the hemoglobin S polymerization inhibitor.

Mitapivat is currently approved as a disease-modifying treatment for anemia in adults with alpha- or beta-thalassemia, and an approval decision in sickle cell disease is expected by February of next year.

Labeling for mitapivat includes a boxed warning due to the risk of liver injury, which also warranted a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) program. The FDA has requested an analysis on whether a REMS would be needed in sickle cell disease, but drugmaker Agios Pharmaceuticals said the data so far have shown no cases of liver injury that follow the pattern or severity seen in the thalassemia trials.

The RISE UP trial was conducted across 69 sites in 15 countries and randomized 207 patients older than 16 years with anemia and recurrent sickle cell pain crises in a 2:1 ratio to twice-daily mitapivat (100 mg) or placebo.

At baseline, participants had a median age of 25 years, 57.5% were female, mean hemoglobin was about 8.5 g/dL, and they averaged 3.4 sickle cell pain crises per year.

The primary endpoint of hemoglobin response was defined as a 1 g/dL or greater increase in average hemoglobin concentration from week 24 to week 52 compared with the baseline.

In a commentary accompanying the study, Jennifer Knight-Madden, MBBS, PhD, and Zachary Ramsay, MBBS, both of the University of the West Indies in Kingston, Jamaica, noted that despite the mixed results on the primary endpoints, "there could be clinical benefit" among the mitapivat responders.

The findings should be interpreted with caution, they noted, but post-hoc analyses suggested the mitapivat-treated participants "who achieved a hemoglobin response experienced lower annualized rates of sickle cell pain crises, fewer related hospitalizations and emergency department visits, longer times to first and second sickle cell pain crises, and lower fatigue scores compared with non-responders."

"The findings provide evidence that a clinically meaningful benefit can exist within a subset of patients," they wrote. "As acknowledged by the authors, this study was not designed to identify patients likely to achieve a hemoglobin response, and differences in hemoglobin response could be due to genetic and epigenetic modifiers, red cell metabolic differences, and co-inherited red cell variants."

As for safety data, mitapivat was associated with lower rates of grade ≥3 adverse events (AEs), at 33% versus 41% with placebo, and lower rates of serious AEs (20% vs 29%), Andemariam and colleagues reported. One of the serious AEs in a mitapivat-treated patient was considered treatment-related, however.

Overall, AEs leading to treatment discontinuation occurred in 4% of patients in the mitapivat group and in 3% of the placebo group. Despite no signal of liver injury in the study, some hepatic-related AEs did lead to mitapivat discontinuation, including one patient with increases in aspartate aminotransferase (grade 3) and bilirubin (grade 2), another patient with hepatic enzyme increases (grade 4) deemed unrelated to treatment, a patient with hepatic cytolysis (grade 2) and other AEs, and one patient with transaminase increases (grade 2) considered secondary to an infection.

Deaths occurred in 2% of the mitapivat arm and 3% of the placebo arm, with none deemed treatment-related.

#5745. Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain

Deep within the brainstem is a tiny group of nerve cells that plays an outsized role in how the brain functions. This region, called the locus coeruleus (LC), gets its name from the Latin words for "blue place." Although it contains only a small fraction of the brain's neurons, it produces norepinephrine (NE), a chemical messenger that helps regulate attention, learning, heart rate, and the body's reactions to stress and excitement.

Scientists have long assumed that the LC operates like a loudspeaker, sending essentially the same norepinephrine signal across the brain. However, a new study published in Nature challenges that understanding. Using brain imaging, recordings of neural activity, genetic techniques, and behavioral experiments in mice, researchers at the Allen Institute discovered that the LC communicates through several distinct pathways. Rather than broadcasting one general message, it delivers signals to specific destinations, with different groups of neurons responding to different experiences.

A Hidden Brain Network That Sends Precise Messages

By tracing the connections of LC neurons, researchers found that different groups of cells communicate with specific regions of the nervous system. These pathways determine where signals trigger the release of norepinephrine, creating a much more organized communication network than previously recognized.

Neurons in the upper (dorsal) portion of the LC primarily connect to the cerebral cortex and forebrain. Meanwhile, cells in the lower (ventral) portion send their signals mainly to the brainstem and spinal cord. This arrangement allows different parts of the LC to influence separate brain functions.

"The findings suggest the brain's norepinephrine system is far more like a targeted postal network than a foghorn," said Karel Svoboda, director of Neural Dynamics at the Allen Institute and study co-author.

Why the Discovery Could Matter for Brain Disorders

Understanding how this signaling network is organized could eventually change how certain neurological and mental health conditions are treated.

Norepinephrine plays a central role in regulating attention and mood, making it an important target for medications used to treat depression, anxiety, and ADHD. Neurons in the LC are also among the earliest brain cells to deteriorate in Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the new findings could have implications for understanding and treating these conditions.

Current treatments that influence norepinephrine can affect multiple brain circuits at once, sometimes producing beneficial effects in one region while causing unwanted effects elsewhere. A clearer map of the LC's specialized pathways could help scientists develop therapies that act more selectively on the circuits involved in particular symptoms.

The research received support from the National Institutes of Health's Brain Research Through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies® Initiative, also known as The BRAIN Initiative®.

Scientists Identify Brain Cells Involved in Learning

The researchers also uncovered an important distinction between the functions of different LC neurons.

Cells in the dorsal LC that connect to the cortex were particularly active during learning. When mice performed decision-making tasks and adjusted their choices after an unfavorable result, these neurons increased their activity.

Neurons in the ventral LC behaved differently. Their activity rose shortly before mice ignored signals indicating that a reward might be available. This suggests that these cells help regulate whether animals respond to opportunities in their surroundings.

"What emerged was a clear map: neurons in the dorsal LC that send signals upward to the cortex are involved in learning, whereas neurons in the ventral region projecting downward to the brainstem and spinal cord govern whether animals engage with their environment at all," said Svoboda. "We also showed that these anatomical differences are mirrored by distinct gene expression patterns."

These findings indicate that the differences between the two groups extend beyond their locations and connections. They also have distinct patterns of gene activity that reflect their specialized roles.

Researchers Discover a Record-Breaking Neuron

The study involved an extensive examination of the mouse brain. Scientists used whole-brain imaging to study nearly 35,000 neurons, analyzed the genetic profiles of almost 400,000 cells, and reconstructed the complete structures of several exceptionally complex nerve cells.

During this work, they encountered another remarkable finding: LC neurons possess extraordinarily long axons. These projections carry signals from nerve cells to other cells, allowing information to travel across the nervous system.

The researchers found that LC axons measured approximately 35 centimeters long on average. One particularly extraordinary axon had a total reconstructed length of 70.32 centimeters, making it part of the longest single neuron ever measured in a mouse.

"This neuron, like many others that we studied, supplies NE to a very large volume of the cerebral cortex. For the brain, this is highly unusual. Most neurons are more specific in their targets," said Jeremiah Cohen, scientist at the Allen Institute and study co-author. "But this neuron doesn't release NE everywhere. It ignores the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord."

Despite its remarkable length and extensive reach, the neuron does not distribute norepinephrine throughout the entire brain. Instead, its connections remain selective, reinforcing the discovery that the LC operates through carefully organized signaling pathways.

A New Understanding of How the Brain Learns

The researchers also identified intriguing similarities between the norepinephrine system and the brain's dopamine signaling system.

Dopamine is another major chemical messenger that sends signals to the basal ganglia, a brain region involved in forming habits. Scientists suspect that dopamine and norepinephrine work together to support learning, potentially allowing the brain to acquire several complex and abstract concepts at the same time.

By revealing the intricate connections, specialized functions, and unusual physical structure of neurons in the locus coeruleus, the research provides a more detailed picture of how the animal brain communicates and learns.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice, they could eventually help scientists better understand human brain function and design treatments that target specific neural circuits rather than affecting entire signaling systems.

#5744. Industry Voices—The other AI divide is already opening in healthcare

Industry Voices—The other AI divide is already opening in healthcare" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The debate over AI and inequality has largely focused on people—who will have access to the technology, who will benefit from it and who risks being left behind. But inside healthcare, another AI divide is already taking shape. This one is between the hospitals that have the money, talent and infrastructure to put AI to work and those that don't.

The numbers are striking. According to federal data on hospital AI adoption, 71% of U.S. hospitals used predictive AI integrated with their electronic health records in 2024. But adoption reached 96% among large hospitals compared with just 59% among small hospitals. Among hospitals belonging to multi-hospital systems, 86% used predictive AI. Among independent hospitals, it was only 37%.

That gap matters because AI is quickly becoming part of how hospitals survive, not simply an innovation project. The same federal data show some of the fastest-growing hospital AI applications are decidedly practical, including billing and scheduling. These are exactly the kinds of labor-intensive functions where financially stressed hospitals need to find efficiencies.

Yet those hospitals may be the least equipped to make the investment.

Hospitals remain extraordinarily dependent on people to operate. According to the American Hospital Association, workforce spending accounted for about 60% of hospital expenses in 2025, exceeding $1 trillion. Total hospital expenses grew 7.5% that year, more than twice the growth in hospital prices.

This creates a dangerous catch-22. The hospitals with the greatest need to use technology to redesign labor-intensive operations frequently have the least capacity to invest in doing so.

A large health system can afford an AI pilot that fails. It can hire an innovation team, absorb a lengthy implementation, build governance and compliance infrastructure, and try again if the economics don't work. A safety-net, community or independent hospital often has far less room for error. A multi-year software contract that might eventually produce savings still requires money today.

And buying the technology is only the beginning.

Successful AI deployment requires workflow redesign, change management, integration, measurement and governance. Even among hospitals already using predictive AI, the federal data show meaningful variation in how comprehensively models are evaluated for accuracy, bias and performance after implementation. Smaller, rural and independent hospitals also continue to lag their larger counterparts in adoption.

If we leave the market to work this out one hospital at a time, we should expect that divide to compound. Systems that successfully automate expensive workflows can reinvest those savings into their next technology investment. They build institutional knowledge. Their employees get better at implementation. They become more attractive partners to technology companies looking for sophisticated customers and proving grounds.

The hospitals that wait don't simply remain where they are. They lose ground. The answer cannot be telling every hospital to develop a better AI strategy. We need to change the ownership and financing model for healthcare AI.

Hospitals already know how to collaborate when acting collectively creates an advantage. Group purchasing organizations allow them to aggregate purchasing power rather than negotiate for every product independently. Clinical research networks allow institutions to pool patients, expertise and infrastructure to answer questions no single organization could address as effectively alone.

We should apply the same instinct to AI. Instead of requiring every health system to independently buy, implement and govern variations of the same technology, health systems should increasingly pool their purchasing power, operational expertise and capital to build common AI capabilities. And smaller, independent and safety-net organizations need a path into those collaborations rather than simply another vendor contract.

The venture community has a responsibility here as well. We need financing structures that acknowledge the economic reality of the organizations that really need to adopt technologies. That could mean performance-based models where payment is tied to verified savings rather than large upfront commitments. It could mean consortium models in which multiple health systems share implementation resources and governance.

And increasingly, it should mean giving health systems ownership in the companies and infrastructure they help create. Ownership matters because the economics of AI are changing quickly. As the technology itself becomes increasingly commoditized, enduring value will come from distribution, proprietary workflows, real-world implementation knowledge and access to the environments where healthcare actually happens. Health systems contribute enormously to each of those things. Under the traditional vendor model, however, they can provide the workflows, clinical expertise and proving ground and then pay someone else an annual fee for the resulting product.

That bargain deserves to be reconsidered. Collective ownership can help address the trust problem, too. AI adoption isn't only a technology decision. It requires decisions about validation, monitoring, clinical safety and who is accountable when something goes wrong. Federal researchers found that hospitals increasingly rely on multiple parties to evaluate AI, with 74% reporting more than one entity accountable for evaluation. Smaller hospitals should not each have to recreate that infrastructure from scratch.

Shared infrastructure could include common validation standards, clinical oversight, monitoring and implementation expertise. That would give more hospitals access not only to AI, but to the capabilities required to deploy it responsibly.

None of this means every hospital needs to own every AI company, or that traditional vendors disappear. It means we should stop assuming that the only scalable model for healthcare innovation is one technology company selling essentially the same capability to thousands of hospitals one contract at a time.

The AI divide between hospitals is already here. If adoption continues to depend primarily on the size of an organization's balance sheet, the institutions best positioned today will keep accumulating advantages while those with the least room for error fall further behind.

AI gives hospitals a real opportunity to break their dependence on increasingly expensive, labor-intensive ways of operating. But the organizations that need that opportunity most cannot be the last ones able to afford it. Preventing that outcome will require more than making AI cheaper. It will require giving more health systems the ability to build, govern and share in the technology's value, transforming them.

AI should become something hospitals build together, not another advantage reserved for those that could already afford to move first.

Amanda DeMano is SVP of venture creation at Abundant Venture Partners.

Editor's Note: Abundant Venture Partners is a strategic investor in the makers of certain AI technologies, including SpendRule and Playback Health.
