#5729. Fierce Healthcare Policy Brief: HHS launches breast cancer screening initiative; RHTP funds flow to 6 states

Fierce Healthcare Policy Brief: HHS launches breast cancer screening initiative; RHTP funds flow to 6 states" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest across Washington, D.C. with this weekly brief. Read below for news from Oct. 26 to Oct. 30.

HHS’ Office on Women’s Health (OWH) announced Tuesday a coordinated initiative with the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) and DenseBreast-info.org (DBI) to improve breast cancer screening and early detection efforts nationwide.

The OWH–AHRQ Breast Cancer Screening and Diagnostic Follow-up Initiative will analyze national screening and follow-up patterns, with more than 40 health systems poised to expand evidence-based practices and address delays in care.

“Women deserve clear information about breast cancer screening options beyond mammography, particularly if they have dense breasts or other risk factors,” said Tammy Huizenga, AHRQ senior advisor for nutrition and women’s health, in a statement. “Understanding their individual risk and available options helps women and their healthcare providers make informed decisions that support earlier detection.”

OWH and DBI will also collaborate through a memorandum of understanding to expand access to evidence-based educational resources aimed at supporting informed discussions between women and providers, promote understanding of screenings and diagnostic follow-up options, and improve breast density awareness.

HHS' health information technology arm finalized a rule that streamlines the health IT certification program, projecting to save billions in compliance costs.

The rule, called Health Data, Technology and Interoperability: ONC Deregulatory Actions to Unleash Prosperity (HTI-5), is projected to save more than $1.5 billion in regulatory costs, according to the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC). Full story.

The Trump administration awarded $233 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to improve healthcare access across California. This investment will help rural providers deliver and coordinate care locally through regional care networks, telehealth, workforce development and upgraded healthcare technology. California has committed its full fiscal year 2026 funding to improve healthcare in rural communities across the state.

The state plans to use the investment to expand rural primary, maternal, specialty and behavioral healthcare; grow the healthcare workforce; expand telehealth and regional care networks; modernize technology and infrastructure; and support new care delivery and payment models, according to a CMS announcement. Regional care networks and telehealth will connect patients with providers and help coordinate care, while partnerships with midwives, doulas and community health workers will support maternal and primary care. Investments will also support education and training pathways to grow the rural healthcare workforce, improve technology and modernize infrastructure.

It is the full amount of funding the state will receive for fiscal year 2026.

CMS doled out $193.7M in RHTP funding to 45 organizations across Florida to expand healthcare access in rural communities, with a particular focus on bringing care closer to patients.

Florida will use the substantial investment to build out telehealth, remote monitoring, mobile and community-based services; increase access to preventive and specialty care; strengthen rural providers and the healthcare workforce; and support new care delivery and payment models.

The state's approach uses telemedicine, remote patient monitoring, pharmacy-based services, diagnostic kiosks and community paramedicine to give patients more ways to access needed care. Partnerships are a defining feature of Florida’s approach, with more than 500 partnerships across the 45 awardees bringing hospitals, clinics, local governments and community organizations together to support statewide rural healthcare transformation, according to CMS in an Oct. 23 announcement.

Florida will receive $209,938,195 in total RHTP funding in fiscal year 2026.

CMS awarded $186 million in funding to improve healthcare access across rural Idaho. This investment will help rural providers deliver and coordinate care locally through modern technology, new care models, an expanded healthcare workforce and improvements to healthcare facilities, the agency announced.

The investment supports five initiatives designed to strengthen healthcare delivery and modernize rural Idaho’s healthcare system. Funding for telehealth, cybersecurity and electronic health record modernization will help rural providers deliver and coordinate care better locally. Investments in community health workers and emergency medical services professionals will help bring services into homes and communities, while training, recruitment and retention efforts will grow Idaho’s rural healthcare workforce. The funding will also support programs addressing chronic disease, behavioral health, maternal and child health as well as improvements to rural healthcare facilities and equipment.

It is the full amount of funding the state will receive for fiscal year 2026.

The Trump administration locked in a regulation that will require pharmacy benefit managers to disclose fees and compensation to self-funded employers.

The rule, finalized by the Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration, aims to ensure that employers can see what drug manufacturers, pharmacies and other entities are paying their PBMs and any affiliated brokers and consultants.

The department said in an announcement that this data will support employers in negotiating contracts and pushing to lower drug costs for their workers and their dependents. Full story

CMS awarded $87 million in RHTP funding to 129 rural healthcare providers through Rural Texas Strong to strengthen healthcare across rural communities. The investment will help improve health outcomes for rural Texans, build a strong healthcare workforce and modernize facilities and equipment across rural Texas, according to an agency announcement.

The funding will help rural providers prevent and manage chronic conditions, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease and chronic respiratory disease; recruit and retain physicians, emergency medical personnel and other healthcare professionals; replace aging medical equipment; and improve existing facilities. Together, these investments will help rural providers maintain essential services and bring quality healthcare closer to home for rural Texans.

Texas is slated to receive $281,319,361 in total RHTP funding in fiscal year 2026.

A Massachusetts judge has sided with a coalition of states in an ongoing lawsuit over the rollout of Medicaid work requirements, and rejected the Trump administration's definition of "medical frailty" for critical exemptions.

Judge Richard Stearns ruled Thursday that a regulation issued over the summer that aimed to offer guardrails to the implementation of the work requirements unlawfully limited the group of people who would qualify as "medically frail" and would thus be exempted.

In the rule, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said that the frailty exemption would apply when a "physical, mental, or other behavioral health condition significantly impairs the individual’s ability to comply with the community engagement requirement."

This runs afoul of existing law, as there are individuals in five frailty categories established by Congress who may not qualify for the exemption under CMS' definition, Stearns said. Full story

Missouri will receive nearly $40 million in RHTP funding to modernize rural healthcare services and expand access to care across the state. The investment will support 26 rural healthcare providers as they renovate, reconfigure, equip or repurpose existing facilities and expand maternal health, behavioral health, diagnostic, outpatient and chronic disease management services across Missouri, according to an announcement.

The funding will support new labor, delivery and private triage rooms; expanded behavioral health services for older adults and people with substance use disorders; and upgraded diagnostic equipment, including MRI, mammography and ultrasound services. The funding will also expand primary care and increase the capacity of rural health clinics, helping rural providers update existing facilities and capabilities to better match the healthcare needs of the communities they serve, CMS said.

In total, Mississippi will receive $216,276,818 during fiscal year 2026.

The Trump Administration announced more than $19 million in RHTP funding through 11 awards to strengthen and modernize healthcare delivery throughout rural West Virginia. The state plans to invest in virtual and specialty care, mobile health services and chronic disease management, growing the rural healthcare workforce and modernizing technology and health data systems.

The investment will support new tools and services across the state, including mobile health units and drone delivery for time-critical medical supplies; remote eye care and patient monitoring technology; nursing education and apprenticeship programs; and secure systems that allow healthcare providers to better share information. Investments will also support mental health and substance use disorder recovery services and tools that reduce administrative burden for healthcare professionals, CMS announced.

West Virginia will receive a total of $199,476,099 in RHTP funding in fiscal year 2026.

#5728. A Pristine 1950s John Lautner ‘Time Capsule’ Just Listed for $2.1M—and It’s Had Only One Owner

Referred to as the Rosemary and Joseph Baldwin Residence, a John Lautner-designed home seeks a new steward in the trendy Los Angeles neighborhood of Silver Lake.

But what’s even more rare is that this three-bedroom, two-bath property spanning 1,679 square feet has had just one owner. With very few updates, it’s a veritable time capsule.

Tucked into a wooded, hillside setting, Lautner balanced the home on posts anchored by shear walls. This creates a floating effect, made even more dramatic with floor-to-ceiling glass and a wraparound deck. That the home is seamlessly integrated into nature, including redwood-plank siding and skylights that coax in nature light, are two other marvels.

“The house is completely original, minus a tree that was growing through the teak deck in the backyard and that needed to be removed,” says Louis Magnano of Modern California House, who is handling the $2,099,999 listing. “It’s about as original as you can get in 2026.”

This includes the entire kitchen as well as lighting fixtures, mahogany paneling, and terrazzo and parquet flooring. As well, the fireplace is original, and all of the windows, too. Each bedroom’s built-ins are also intact. The living room’s inverted-pyramid ceiling and triangular clerestory windows are also striking.

“It’s completely original, which is very rare for these types of homes in L.A.,” says Magnano.

“They get traded (and) things are done to them when they shouldn’t be. This house doesn’t have that. Whoever is going to purchase this home and be the next steward will need to restore and bring it up to today’s standards but while maintaining the original quality of the home. The sellers want to see it restored.”

This could mean updating the systems, for starters.

How often does a Lautner-designed home hop onto the market, though?

“They have been coming up quite frequently for sale in the last few years,” says Magnano, “but there’s so few and far between, maybe it’s just a special time in the marketplace.”

In 1955, Lautner—a Taliesin Fellow under Frank Lloyd Wright during the 1930s—was commissioned by commercial artist James Baldwin and his wife Rosemary to create their family home, utilizing a 7,491-square-foot lot. Rosemary’s sister introduced them to Lautner.

Lautner’s residence (Silvertop) is on the same street as the Baldwin home.

“Silver Lake is really known for a lot of its architectural history, not only by John Lautner, but Richard Neutra, Rudolph Schinder, to name a few starchitects,” says Magnano.

Lautner would later design three other Southern California homes that put him on the map: The Chemosphere (1960), The Sheats-Goldstein Residence (1961-1963) and The Elrod Residence (1968).

“The Baldwin Residence marks a pivotal moment in that career: its siting, spatial progression, and detail recall Wright, even as they reveal Lautner's own emerging voice,” reads the listing, adding that this is “an authentic piece of Los Angeles architectural history and a rare stewardship opportunity that may not come again.”

In addition to the striking interior design, another wow-worthy feature are views of the Hollywood Hills and San Gabriel Mountains.

What will also likely attract buyers is the location. As a haven for artists, it’s similar to the type of community that drew the Baldwins there back in the 1950s.

“Silver Lake has a very rich artist community and it’s vibrant, with young people, and there’s new cafes and a lot of nightlife happening in the area,” says Magnano. “There’s a lot of development happening in Silver Lake and a big restoration project taking place in the reservoir that the city of Los Angeles is getting ready to break ground on soon, to beautify the area.”

The ideal buyer, he says, is “somebody who understands the significance of these historical properties, who wants to restore them and honor them and keep them in the original glory that they all are. It was a family home for the Baldwins. They had three children. It could be a family home (again) but it could be somebody’s second home or ‘home away from home.’”

Based in Milwaukee, Kristine Hansen writes for TravelandLeisure.com, ArchitecturalDigest.com, Vogue.com, and other outlets. She’s also the author of “Frank Lloyd Wright’s Wisconsin: How America’s Most Famous Architect Found Inspiration in His Home State.” She lives in a 1924 bungalow.

#5727. Scientists discover a hidden switch that burns fat and blocks new fat cells

Scientists have identified a remarkable protein switch that influences whether cells burn fat or store it. Disabling this protein increases fat consumption and interferes with the formation of new fat cells, raising the possibility of a different approach to treating obesity. Subsequent research has strengthened the discovery, revealing that the same protein helps regulate how much energy the body burns.

What if one of the keys to fighting obesity lies not in suppressing appetite, but in changing how the body's cells use energy?

Researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science have identified a protein called MTCH2, nicknamed "Mitch," that plays an important role in controlling metabolism. When scientists disabled this protein in laboratory experiments, cells began consuming more fuel, including fats and carbohydrates. They also found that removing Mitch could interfere with the process through which immature cells develop into fat cells.

The discovery builds on earlier experiments in mice, in which switching off Mitch in muscle tissue increased energy expenditure, improved endurance, and protected the animals from diet-related obesity.

The findings, published in The EMBO Journal in January 2025, suggest that manipulating this protein could eventually offer a way to influence both fat burning and fat accumulation. Additional research published later that year has provided further evidence of its importance in regulating body fat and metabolism.

Why Scientists Are Searching for Better Obesity Treatments

Over the past decade, medications designed to promote weight loss have transformed obesity treatment. Drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide have helped many patients achieve substantial reductions in body weight, largely by influencing appetite and the body's responses to food.

But losing weight does not necessarily mean losing only fat.

Weight reduction can also involve a decline in lean body mass, which includes muscle and other tissues. Preserving muscle is especially important because it supports strength, mobility, and metabolic health.

A 2026 analysis of 20 clinical trials involving 15,782 participants found that lean mass accounted for approximately 25% to 39% of the weight lost with several widely used weight-loss medications. Importantly, the researchers found that comparable proportional losses also occurred with lifestyle interventions, while adding resistance training helped preserve more lean tissue.

These concerns have encouraged scientists to investigate ways to reduce body fat while protecting the muscles needed for long-term health.

Professor Atan Gross and his colleagues at the Weizmann Institute arrived at a possible avenue through an unexpected discovery involving Mitch.

Switching Off One Protein Protected Mice From Obesity

In earlier experiments, Gross's team reduced the activity of MTCH2 in the muscles of mice. The effects were striking.

The genetically modified animals showed increased metabolic activity and were resistant to obesity caused by their diet. Their muscles also developed more fibers with a high capacity for using oxygen, helping improve physical endurance.

The mice performed better in exercise and stress tests and showed improvements in heart function. In addition to resisting excess fat accumulation, they experienced favorable changes in their overall body composition.

The results suggested that Mitch was doing much more than controlling a single metabolic reaction. Somehow, this protein appeared to influence the body's ability to use energy, store fat, and sustain physical activity.

That raised an intriguing question: How could disabling one protein produce such widespread effects?

To investigate, the researchers turned their attention to mitochondria, the microscopic structures responsible for supplying much of the energy that cells need to function.

The Mitochondria Connection Behind Fat Burning

Mitochondria are frequently described as the powerhouses of cells because they convert energy from food into a usable form called ATP, or adenosine triphosphate.

ATP acts as a cellular energy currency. Muscles use it to contract, cells need it to grow and repair themselves, and countless biological processes depend on a steady supply.

However, mitochondria are not static structures. They constantly change shape, joining together into larger networks or separating into smaller units.

When mitochondria fuse, they can form interconnected systems that help coordinate energy production. When they divide, the resulting structures may operate differently, altering how efficiently cells produce and consume energy.

Gross's team had previously established that Mitch plays a major role in mitochondrial fusion, the process that allows separate mitochondria to merge.

Without this protein, the mitochondrial network becomes fragmented. Although the cells can still generate energy, they experience changes in energy efficiency and demand that can force them to consume more fuel.

This offered a possible explanation for the unusual metabolism observed in the mice. Instead of conserving energy efficiently, their cells appeared to be operating in a more energy-intensive state.

But would disabling Mitch have a similar effect in human cells?

Human Cells Begin Burning More Fat Without Mitch

To answer that question, researchers led by doctoral student Sabita Chourasia used genetic engineering to remove MTCH2 from human cells grown in the laboratory.

The change disrupted the normal structure of their mitochondrial networks. Individual mitochondria became more separated, and the balance between energy production and energy demand shifted.

The cells developed a persistent shortage of readily available energy relative to their needs, even as their mitochondria increased their oxygen-consuming activity.

To compensate, they began consuming more nutrients.

"After deleting Mitch, we examined, every few hours, the effect that had on more than 100 substances taking part in metabolism in human cells," Chourasia explains. "We saw an increase in cellular respiration, the process in which the cell produces energy from nutrients, such as carbohydrates and fats, using oxygen. This explains the increase in muscular endurance in previous experiments using mice."

Cellular respiration is the series of chemical reactions that allows cells to extract usable energy from nutrients. Increasing this activity generally requires a greater supply of fuel.

The researchers found that cells lacking Mitch consumed more fats, carbohydrates, and amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.

Fat metabolism was particularly revealing.

Rather than relying on their usual mix of energy sources, the altered cells increased their use of fatty acids for fuel. This indicated that MTCH2 influences not only how much energy cells consume, but also which nutrients they use to meet that demand.

"We discovered that deleting Mitch led to a major drop in fats in membranes," Gross explains. "At the same time, we saw an increase in fatty substances used to produce energy, and we realized that the fat was being broken down from the membrane to be used as fuel. In other words, we showed that Mitch determines the fate of fat in human cells."

Cell membranes are thin, flexible barriers made largely from fatty molecules called lipids. They protect cells and organize many of their essential functions.

The findings suggested that cells deprived of Mitch were changing how they distributed and used these lipids, drawing on some of their available fatty resources to support increased energy consumption.

Detailed analysis also revealed changes in stored lipids, demonstrating that the effect was more complex than simply eliminating cellular fat. Overall, the results showed that MTCH2 is a powerful regulator of how cells allocate nutrients between energy production and other biological needs.

The researchers then investigated whether Mitch also influences how fat cells develop.

This question was particularly interesting because previous studies had found elevated MTCH2 levels in fat tissue from women with obesity.

Fat cells, also known as adipocytes, do not appear fully formed. They develop from immature precursor cells through a process called adipogenesis, or fat cell differentiation.

As these precursor cells mature, they must build new cellular structures, produce fats, and activate genes that allow them to specialize in storing energy.

All of this requires considerable energy and raw materials.

Gross's team suspected that removing Mitch might disrupt the process by creating an environment in which cells were too busy consuming fuel to build the components needed for fat storage.

Experiments using mouse precursor fat cells supported this idea. When the researchers deleted MTCH2, far fewer cells successfully developed into mature fat cells.

In the published experiments, approximately 80% to 90% of normal precursor cells differentiated within six days, compared with only 5% to 10% of cells lacking MTCH2. The altered cells also accumulated substantially fewer lipid droplets, the structures used to store fat.

"When we deleted Mitch from the progenitor cells, we discovered that the environment created in these cells was not conducive to the synthesis of new fats," Gross explains. "Reducing the ability to synthesize membranes prevents the cells from growing, developing and reaching the point where differentiation is possible. The process of fat accumulation requires a large amount of available energy, but in cells without Mitch, there is a shortage of energy. In addition, the expression of genes necessary for differentiation is suppressed, and there is a shortage of the substances vital for this process to occur. As a result, differentiation of new fat cells is reduced, along with fat accumulation."

In other words, disabling Mitch appeared to affect fat metabolism in two distinct ways. It increased the consumption of energy-rich nutrients and interfered with the cellular machinery needed to develop new fat-storing cells.

Importantly, the fat cell differentiation experiments used a mouse-derived cell line, while the detailed analysis of nutrient consumption was conducted in human cells. The combined results suggest a broader role for the protein, but they do not establish that blocking MTCH2 would prevent new fat cells from forming in people.

Follow-Up Research Reveals Another Fat-Burning Mechanism

The importance of MTCH2 became even clearer in research published on October 3, 2025, in Nature Communications.

An international research team, which included Gross and Chourasia, investigated how MTCH2 influences metabolism in fat tissue. By analyzing human and mouse fat samples, studying cultured fat cells, and conducting experiments in genetically modified mice, the scientists identified another mechanism linking this protein to energy expenditure.

They found that MTCH2 helps regulate the movement of fatty acids into mitochondria, where these molecules can be broken down to produce energy.

The process involves an enzyme called carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1, or CPT1. This enzyme acts as an important checkpoint, helping determine how much fat can enter mitochondria for use as fuel.

Normally, CPT1 activity is regulated by a molecule called malonyl-CoA, which signals when cells should limit fatty acid consumption.

The researchers discovered that MTCH2 physically interacts with CPT1 and influences how strongly this regulatory signal affects the enzyme.

Removing MTCH2 altered that control system, allowing mitochondria to increase fatty acid utilization and energy expenditure.

This provided a more detailed molecular explanation for why disabling the protein could encourage cells to burn additional fat.

Mice Burned More Energy Without Eating Less

The follow-up study also produced an especially promising result.

When researchers removed MTCH2 specifically from the fat cells of mice, the animals burned more energy without increasing their physical activity or changing how much food they consumed.

Under a regular diet, the genetically modified mice gained weight at a rate similar to that of normal mice.

However, when the animals were fed a high-fat diet, a difference emerged.

Mice lacking MTCH2 in their fat tissue gained less weight and accumulated less body fat than untreated mice, despite consuming similar amounts of food.

Their lean body mass remained comparable to that of the control animals.

The genetically modified mice also demonstrated improved glucose tolerance, indicating that their bodies were better able to manage blood sugar after receiving glucose. In addition, their cholesterol levels were lower.

These findings strengthened the evidence that MTCH2 influences whole-body metabolism, rather than simply changing the behavior of isolated cells.

The scientists also found that its metabolic effects could occur independently of UCP1, a protein commonly associated with heat production in brown fat. Brown fat is a specialized form of body fat that helps generate heat by burning energy, whereas white fat primarily stores excess energy.

Discovering an additional pathway for increasing energy expenditure could be important because it offers researchers another potential target for treating obesity and related metabolic disorders.

Could This Protein Lead to Better Weight-Loss Treatments?

Together, the findings suggest that MTCH2 may be an important molecular switch linking fat storage, energy consumption, and the development of fat cells.

The original experiments showed that removing the protein could increase nutrient consumption in human cells and interfere with fat cell formation in mouse cells. The later research demonstrated that selectively removing MTCH2 from fat tissue could increase energy expenditure and protect mice against excessive weight gain on a high-fat diet.

That combination raises the possibility of developing treatments that change how the body handles energy, potentially complementing medications that primarily work by reducing appetite.

However, several major questions remain unanswered.

Scientists have not yet demonstrated that inhibiting MTCH2 produces safe, sustained weight loss in humans. The protein also participates in other important biological activities, including mitochondrial regulation and pathways involved in cell survival. Blocking it throughout the body could therefore produce unwanted consequences.

Preventing fat cells from forming is not necessarily beneficial in every situation, either. Healthy fat tissue plays an essential role in storing excess energy, maintaining blood sugar balance, and producing hormones. Disrupting its function could potentially redirect fats into organs where they may cause harm.

Researchers will need to determine whether MTCH2 can be targeted safely, which tissues would benefit most, and whether reducing its activity would preserve muscle health while promoting fat loss.

For now, established strategies such as resistance exercise and adequate protein intake remain important for protecting muscle during weight reduction. A 2026 review of clinical trials found that combining lifestyle changes with resistance training produced a more favorable pattern of lean mass preservation than weight-loss interventions without such exercise.

The research nevertheless points toward a compelling possibility: Rather than focusing exclusively on how much food the body takes in, future obesity treatments might also influence how cells decide whether to burn energy or store it.

And one protein, Mitch, appears to be deeply involved in that decision.

The original study, titled "MTCH2 controls energy demand and expenditure to fuel anabolism during adipogenesis," was published in The EMBO Journal on January 3, 2025.

The research was led by Sabita Chourasia and Professor Atan Gross at the Weizmann Institute of Science.

Additional contributors included Dr. Christopher Petucci, Clarissa Shoffler, and Dina Abbasian from the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia; Hu Wang and Professor Xianlin Han from the University of Texas at San Antonio; Dr. Ehud Sivan, Dr. Alexander Brandis, Tevie Mehlman, Dr. Sergey Malitsky, Dr. Maxim Itkin, Dr. Ayala Sharp, Dr. Ron Rotkopf, and Dr. Bareket Dassa from Weizmann's Life Sciences Core Facilities Department; and Dr. Limor Regev and Dr. Yehudit Zaltsman from Weizmann's Immunology and Regenerative Biology Department.

The follow-up study, "MTCH2 modulates CPT1 activity to regulate lipid metabolism of adipocytes," was published in Nature Communications on October 3, 2025. It involved an international collaboration, including researchers affiliated with ETH Zurich, Weizmann Institute of Science, and other institutions.

#5726. Opinion: What a mother’s 1834 letter about measles tells us about MAHA

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Downs is the author of “Medicine by the People: How Ordinary People Changed American Healthcare.”

On Sept. 23, I sat in a small glass reading room at Yale’s medical library, turning the rag-paper pages of the Medical Dissenter, a London journal from the 1830s. At the bottom of one page, under the headline, “Report from Mrs. Butt to Mr. Hudson,” I met Jane Butt. Her letter was dated Sept. 23, 1834. I was reading it 192 years later to the day.

Jane lived in the village of Broughton and explained that measles had spread through the children around her earlier that year. She described how one of her own children had caught it. She then reported 36 other cases in her community. Some, she noted, developed severe inflammation of the lungs, one of the complications that can make measles deadly. She believed a cold east wind aggravated their symptoms. Nevertheless, she reported, all of them recovered.

Jane attributed the recoveries to Morison’s pills. James Morison was a merchant with no medical training who believed that a purgative could expel “impure blood” from the body and restore its natural balance. She administered the pills to the sick — sometimes twice a day — and gave as many as six at once to a toddler not yet 2 years old. She also gave the pills to women and, later, to their newborns, she wrote.

Morison’s followers called themselves Hygeists and attacked physicians as a monopoly that bled and poisoned its patients, which was not inaccurate in the 1830s. Much of medicine before the advent of germ theory and bacteriology provided incorrect diagnoses and problematic treatments.

When Jane wrote her letter, women could not train as physicians and were being displaced as midwives by the growing professional authority of doctors. She lacked medical credentials or the authority that came with them, but the Hygeist movement gave her a platform and a space to speak. She said that because “so much [was] said and done to prejudice the public mind against Mr. Morison’s most invaluable medicine,” she was left with no choice.

The journal that printed Jane’s letter sold the cure she praised. The office of the Medical Dissenter on the Strand was one of Morison’s official London depots for the pills in 1837. The same periodical mocked Edward Jenner, who had effectively used cowpox as a vaccination for smallpox, and ridiculed “vaccinic mania.”

After reading Jane’s story, I pulled out my iPhone and took photos of it, which I turned into a PDF. As a historian of medicine, I have seen cases of measles often in historical sources from the Civil War to life among the poor in tenement houses, but when I read those cases measles had long been the province of the past.

As I read Jane’s letter measles was back and raging in my home state of Pennsylvania, where six measles-associated deaths have been reported and federal health officials have disputed how many of them to count. In 2026, the United States has already recorded more than 4,500 measles cases, the largest number since 1991. Last school year, a record 4.2% of kindergartners were exempted from at least one required vaccine, and coverage for the measles vaccine fell to 92.4%, below the level needed to keep outbreaks from spreading. In some communities, the percentages of children who are vaccinated are far lower.

The current explosion of measles in the present had changed how I see the past. I didn’t preserve Jane’s story to indict her or to provide an antecedent to the unfounded arguments against vaccination, which have directly harmed innocent children. I documented her story instead because I had just finished a book on the ways ordinary people changed health care in the United States, and yet their stories have often been neglected, marginalized, or perceived to interfere with the real work of physicians. I wrote the book to show that medical knowledge is not an unalloyed concept created by professionals, but that ordinary people have continually provided evidence, offered interpretations, or even, in the case of Jane, simply counted the number of people who were sick in their communities.

Today, health populism takes shape in the Make America Healthy Again movement, which is rooted in part in grievances over how medical authority has dismissed patients, especially women. According to Politico, MAHA is “made up largely of women who followed Robert F. Kennedy Jr. into the MAGA fold.” Many of these women are moms. MAHA has, in turn, capitalized on the chauvinism of medical authority that began nearly 200 years ago that dismissed women as caregivers and often neglected their insights, their concerns, and their fears about epidemics.

The very act of counting, which might seem obvious or like a natural response to an epidemic, was part of a broader movement that eventually provided a framework for public health. Long before epidemiology developed as a discipline, patients and practitioners observed contagion — that disease seemed to spread from person to person, through households and across villages and nations. Before there was an official public health authority to count, people counted. Counting was also a move toward empiricism. It offered a bird’s-eye view of an epidemic and could provide local physicians or municipal authorities with some sense of the extent of an outbreak.

Counting mattered more than it might seem. Jane lived between two ways of explaining illness. In 1832, when a cholera pandemic reached New York City, clergy called for a national day of fasting and prayer. President Andrew Jackson refused to proclaim one, citing the separation of church and state, so states and churches held their own. Meanwhile, the city published daily counts of the sick and the dead. As the historian Charles Rosenberg showed in “The Cholera Years,” Americans read the epidemic as a judgment on sin even as they tracked it case by case. Jane blamed the wind and thanked God for her family’s recoveries, and she counted, reflecting the beginning of the shift from supernatural explanations to an empirical rationale. Documenting which children grew sickest and following an illness from house to house was a method aimed at articulating an explainable pattern. That method was not dissimilar to what physicians, ship surgeons, and military officials did in the first half of the 19th century when an epidemic erupted.

Jane’s method of dosing pills suffered from one problem: She did not observe what happened if a child did not receive the pills. Most children who caught measles in 1834 survived it, with or without pills. Thirty-seven recoveries indicated to her that the pills worked. They could not tell her what the pills did, or whether children like that toddler recovered despite them. Around the same time, the Paris physician Pierre Louis was also counting patients, and his numbers challenged bloodletting, one of medicine’s most trusted treatments, as a treatment for pneumonia. Louis asked what happened to comparable patients treated differently.

The vaccine does what Jane believed her pills did, and it was tested in ways her pills never were. Parents who refuse it are making Jane’s mistake in reverse.  She credited a cure that did nothing. They discount a protection that works, because measles has become a stranger.

Jane wrote her letter two years after the Provincial Medical and Surgical Association, a precursor to the British Medical Association, was founded in 1832 and more than a decade before the American Medical Association was founded in 1847 — a period in which men on both sides of the Atlantic were defining themselves as the institutional medical authority.

Ordinary people have been actively involved in the conversation since the beginning, but the medical populism of MAHA is making it appear as a new, novel, and even groundbreaking rebellion. Jane’s document reveals that ordinary people’s ideas have often been part of medicine, but medical authority has grown in ways that make them appear as dissenting.

Jane could not be heard in traditional medical circles. Sexism landed her in a fringe periodical, and her endorsement of the quackery of purgatives gave her a headline.

If men had not systematically excluded women from medicine and had recognized that ordinary people’s ideas, insights, and concerns are part of it, Jane might not have reached for purgative pills, and women today might not be reaching for pyrotechnic platforms to be heard.

I have been trained not to write in the conditional tense but instead to explain what happened and how it all went down. I wasn’t looking for her. I found her by accident, but I am drawn to ordinary people’s stories. That’s why I found Jane’s letter so appealing. Before I contextualized it and realized it was part of a radical publication, I was amazed to see the name of a woman in a headline in boldface in a rare book.

Although Jane does not appear in my book, she embodies its thesis — even though her method was wrong. In fact, much of medical practice was wrong or ineffective before the late 19th century, and plenty remained so afterward. There were many ordinary people, like Jane, who witnessed outbreaks and illness in their communities and reported what they saw.

When I closed the volume containing Jane’s letter and walked out of the secure room, through the Victorian reading room, through the rotunda, and past the portraits of physicians whose names circle its walls, Jane’s name was not there, nor were those of any other women from 200 years ago.

It does not have to continue to be that way. Ordinary people’s voices matter and they often begin not in the throes of a national polemic or screamed through a speaker at a MAHA rally but begin, like Jane, with an observation of a child’s health.

Jim Downs is the author of “Medicine by the People: How Ordinary People Changed American Healthcare” (W. W. Norton, October 2026). He is the Gilder Lehrman–NEH professor of history at Gettysburg College and a visiting faculty fellow at Brown University’s Center for the Study of Race and Ethnicity in America. He is a 2025–26 Guggenheim fellow.

#5725. Who’s responsible when clinical AI goes wrong? AMA weighs in

Who’s responsible when clinical AI goes wrong? AMA weighs in" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Building on its recent guidance for organizations’ use and governance of clinical AI, the American Medical Association on Thursday gave a deeper breakdown of how it believes different parties should be responsible for decisions, actions and failures involving the technology.

The latest framework from AMA’s Center for Digital Health and AI addresses liability issues the group said are currently unanswered by existing liability frameworks. Those structures, it said, could leave physicians facing "liability for risks they cannot reasonably prevent, while patients may struggle to seek remedies when AI causes harm."

Other key issues with the status quo liability frameworks, AMA said, are ambiguity around when product liability applies to AI; how contract terms and disclaimers from developers can distance responsibility from risk control; and whether deploying healthcare organizations hold various responsibilities specific to AI, such as local testing or outcomes monitoring.

AMA said the clinical AI liability framework it’s advancing "recognizes that multiple parties may bear liability for the use of AI when something goes wrong," and then aligns that accountability based on a party’s ability to prevent harm. Responsibility is spread out in areas where control is shared, but it does not become interchangeable, and no party’s obligations disappear because another party also bears some,” AMA wrote in a brief outlining its thinking.

As for the physicians AMA represents, the liability framework calls for doctors to "be responsible for the clinical judgment they can meaningfully exercise, based on the system’s intended use, known limitations and the information available at the point of care."

The group also said that oversight from a physician "cannot substitute for adequate evidence, appropriate system design or the conditions necessary to make clinical review meaningful." Physicians should also retain the authority to decline an unproven AI system, or those "whose clinical validation, usefulness or place in the standard of care remains uncertain," without penalty from their organization, AMA said.

"Patients must have meaningful avenues for recourse when clinical AI causes harm, and physicians must be able to use these technologies with confidence that responsibility reflects what they can reasonably know and control," AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., president of the AMA, said in a release on the liability framework. "As AI assumes more clinical functions, developers, healthcare organizations and physicians each have important responsibilities. We need clear expectations that protect patients, support sound clinical judgment, and ensure accountability remains with those best positioned to prevent harm."

The liability framework breaks down in detail one aspect of a broader clinical AI governance framework unveiled by AMA and its Center earlier this month. Those principles and focus areas will guide how AMA works with providers and stakeholders as it tackles issues like licensure and regulation for the fast-moving technology.

"We cannot afford to wait for these questions to be answered through trial and error in patient care," AMA CEO John Whyte, M.D., told Fierce Healthcare of the efforts earlier this month. "The AMA's new framework sets out our ambitious agenda to address these questions. … It will guide our work with physicians, patients, technology developers and policymakers to ensure clinical authority is earned through evidence, how oversight must evolve with risk, and how accountability is maintained."

#5724. Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain

A new study suggests that the Mediterranean diet may protect the heart, brain, and aging cells through a surprising biological mechanism involving tiny proteins produced by mitochondria, the structures responsible for generating most of the energy our cells need.

Researchers at the USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology discovered that people who more closely followed the Mediterranean diet had higher levels of two mitochondrial microproteins called humanin and SHMOOSE. Both have previously been linked to protection against cardiovascular disease and neurodegeneration, the gradual deterioration of nerve cells that occurs in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.

The study, led by USC Leonard Davis Instructional Associate Professor of Gerontology Roberto Vicinanza, offers a possible explanation for how everyday food choices influence cellular health and the aging process.

"These microproteins may act as molecular messengers that translate what we eat into how our cells function and age," Vicinanza said. "It's a new biological pathway that helps explain why the Mediterranean diet is so powerful."

How the Mediterranean Diet May Protect Aging Cells

The Mediterranean diet emphasizes foods such as olive oil, fish, beans, lentils, fruits, and vegetables. It has consistently been associated with a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and cognitive decline. However, scientists are still working to understand exactly how this eating pattern produces its wide-ranging health benefits.

To investigate, the researchers examined blood samples from older adults who followed the Mediterranean diet to different degrees. Those whose eating habits most closely matched the diet had significantly higher concentrations of humanin and SHMOOSE.

They also showed lower indicators of oxidative stress, a process in which harmful molecules called reactive oxygen species overwhelm the body's protective defenses. Over time, oxidative stress can damage proteins, DNA, and other cellular components, contributing to aging and chronic disease.

Interestingly, the researchers found that certain foods were associated with different microproteins. Higher consumption of olive oil, fish, and legumes was linked to increased humanin levels. Meanwhile, olive oil consumption and eating fewer refined carbohydrates were associated with higher levels of SHMOOSE.

Refined carbohydrates include foods made with heavily processed grains and sugars, such as white bread, pastries, and many sugary snacks. These foods generally contain less fiber and fewer naturally occurring nutrients than their minimally processed counterparts.

"These findings suggest that specific components of the Mediterranean diet may directly influence mitochondrial biology," said USC Leonard Davis School Dean and USC Distinguished Professor Pinchas Cohen, the study's senior author. "Humanin and SHMOOSE could serve as biomarkers for adherence to the Mediterranean diet and have clinical significance."

Biomarkers are measurable biological indicators that can provide information about a person's health or physiological state. In this case, the researchers suggest that humanin and SHMOOSE could eventually help scientists understand how closely someone's diet aligns with healthy eating patterns and how their cells respond.

Tiny Mitochondrial Proteins With Powerful Effects

The findings extend a scientific effort spanning more than 20 years to investigate small proteins produced by mitochondria. Cohen has played a leading role in discovering and studying these molecules, which are increasingly recognized as important participants in cellular health.

Mitochondria are often described as the powerhouses of cells because they produce much of the energy required for essential biological activities. But their role extends beyond energy production. They also help regulate metabolism, cellular stress responses, and processes associated with aging.

Unlike most proteins, which are produced using instructions stored in the DNA inside the cell's nucleus, mitochondrial microproteins originate from genetic instructions within mitochondria themselves.

These instructions are found in small segments of mitochondrial DNA known as open reading frames. Some of these regions were once considered nonfunctional, but researchers have discovered that they can encode biologically active molecules.

One of the best understood is humanin, first identified by Cohen and fellow researchers in 2003. Subsequent studies have associated humanin with improved insulin sensitivity, better cardiovascular health, increased longevity, and protection of cognitive abilities.

Insulin sensitivity refers to how effectively the body's cells respond to insulin, the hormone that helps regulate blood sugar. Maintaining healthy insulin sensitivity is important for metabolic health and reducing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Another intriguing microprotein is SHMOOSE (Small Human Mitochondrial ORF Over SErine tRNA), which was identified more recently by Cohen's research team.

SHMOOSE has attracted particular interest because of its possible role in protecting the brain. Scientists have found that a genetic variant of SHMOOSE is associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. The normal version, meanwhile, appears to help protect neurons from damage involving amyloid, a protein that can accumulate abnormally in the brains of people with Alzheimer's.

"These peptides are emerging as key regulators of aging biology," Cohen said. "They connect mitochondrial function to diseases like Alzheimer's and heart disease and now, potentially, to nutrition."

A Hidden Mechanism for Protecting the Heart

The scientists also identified a potentially important connection between humanin and an enzyme called Nox2, which helps generate reactive oxygen species.

Although these molecules have useful roles in normal cell signaling and immune defense, excessive production can contribute to oxidative stress and damage blood vessels and other tissues.

The researchers observed that people with higher humanin levels tended to have lower Nox2 activity. This relationship raises the possibility that humanin helps limit damaging oxidative processes, potentially offering an additional layer of cardiovascular protection.

Based on these findings, the researchers propose that the Mediterranean diet could support heart health in two complementary ways. The diet may help reduce oxidative stress directly while also supporting the production of mitochondrial microproteins that influence pathways involved in cellular damage.

However, the observed associations do not establish that the diet directly increases these proteins or that the proteins themselves prevent cardiovascular disease.

"This could represent a new cardioprotective mechanism of the Mediterranean diet," Vicinanza said.

Bringing the Mediterranean Diet to a Global Audience

Vicinanza's interest in the Mediterranean diet extends beyond investigating its effects inside the body. He has also worked to promote this traditional eating pattern internationally as a way to support human health, cultural heritage, and environmental sustainability.

As part of those efforts, he collaborated with the Municipality of Pollica in Italy, which is recognized as a UNESCO Mediterranean Diet emblematic community.

That collaboration helped support the establishment of the International Day of the Mediterranean Diet through the United Nations.

Observed every year on November 16, the international event is intended to draw attention to the Mediterranean diet's health benefits as well as its cultural traditions and environmental significance.

For Vicinanza, the new findings reinforce the relationship between traditional food practices and modern discoveries about how the body functions.

"We're connecting centuries-old dietary traditions with cutting-edge molecular biology," Vicinanza said. "It supports the idea that healthy eating patterns with little to no ultra-processed foods reflect how humans have eaten over long periods and may create conditions to which mitochondria -- ancient cellular organelles -- are likely adapted."

Could Tiny Proteins Help Unlock Healthier Aging?

Although the findings are promising, the researchers emphasize that the study was relatively small and observational. That means it identified relationships between dietary habits and biological measurements but could not determine whether eating a Mediterranean diet directly caused the differences in microprotein levels.

Other factors, including participants' overall health and lifestyle, could also influence the results.

Nevertheless, the discovery opens an intriguing possibility for the emerging field of precision nutrition, which seeks to develop dietary recommendations based on an individual's biological characteristics and needs.

If future research confirms that dietary changes can reliably influence humanin, SHMOOSE, and related microproteins, these molecules could potentially become useful tools for evaluating nutritional interventions and developing more personalized strategies for healthy aging.

The next step is to determine whether adopting a Mediterranean-style diet actually increases these proteins and whether those changes lead to measurable improvements in cardiovascular health, brain function, or disease risk.

"Our goal is to move from observing associations to understanding causality," Vicinanza said. "If we can harness these pathways, we may be able to design nutritional strategies that promote healthy aging at the molecular level."

The work was funded by the USC Daryl and Irwin Simon Nutrition for Alzheimer's Disease Prevention Research Fund (to Vicinanza), the Hanson-Thorell Family Research Award (to Vicinanza), National Institutes of Health grant P30AG094848 (to Cohen) and PRIN 2022 grant 000031_23_PP_PIGNATELLI_PRIN_2022-B53D23021240006 (to Pignatelli).

#5723. The persisting paradox of men’s health

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Annalisa (Nalis) Merelli is focused on boys’ and men’s health: She looks into reproductive health, trending treatments, screening approaches, mental health, and everything in between.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Buongiorno! As you put the final touches on your Halloween costumes, here is a spooky story for you: Imagine going to urgent care for something as trivial as a UTI, and getting a bill for $1,756, on top of $211 you already paid at the clinic! Keep reading to learn more.

Intuitive Health, a private equity-backed company that runs about 50 hybrid ER-urgent care clinics, was launched on the idea that it could offer an alternative to costly hospital visits, providing under the same roof a clinic for uncomplicated issues and an ER in case of necessity.

But for many patients, the opposite has happened: They came in with simple, urgent care-appropriate conditions but were billed for ER services — think close to $2,000 for an UTI or $7,000 ($2,100 after insurance) for congestion and cough. Company officials say every patient should be asked to sign a form before the “upgrade,” but Tara Bannow found in her investigation this was far from standard practice.

A federal judge in Massachusetts has rejected the federal government’s definition of “medical frailty,” ruling that states didn’t have enough time to assess eligibility status. The decision overturns an interim CMS rule that substantially limited the pool of people eligible for exemptions to the work requirements, in particular by requiring that medically frail people demonstrate that their condition prevents them from working. The rule also didn’t list conditions that would automatically be exempt from work requirements.

The lawsuit was brought on by states claiming that CMS didn’t have the authority to narrow the definition of medically frail, and that the rule would create red tape for beneficiaries having to demonstrate their status, as well as an additional burden for state workers. Thursday’s ruling complicates the already tangled web of work requirements, and might lead to a delay in their rollout past the beginning of 2027, when they were slated to go into effect. More here.

At a rally for Zach Lahn, the farmer-turned-unlikely Republican candidate for Iowa governor, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. called Lahn’s opposition to Big Agriculture, a key tenet of his platform, a “spiritual battle.”

“We have to figure out a way to grow food without poisoning our kids, without giving ourselves cancer, without destroying the soils that enrich us and enrich our microbiome that connect our brain and all of our organs. And make us healthy, robust and vibrant people,” Kennedy told the crowd.

Chelsea Cirruzzo, who reported on the rally, also takes a broader look at RFK Jr.’s big talking points, with the midterms around the corner: fighting fraud, doubling down on “medical freedom” in the form of vaccine choice, and pushing MAHA, even as the political future of the movement looks shaky. (Also don’t forget to check out our 2026 midterms roundup for the most important political news.)

People who are diagnosed with colorectal cancer earlier in life, especially younger than 35, often have a grimmer prognosis than people who develop the disease older. Researchers have been trying to understand why. A new “atlas” of 189 colorectal cancer tumors from patients in their 20s to their 90s could help explain the differences in the disease, while controlling for variables that may have confounded previous studies.

“It is devastating to care for young patients diagnosed with often advanced stages of colorectal cancer. These are people in the prime of their life,” Kimmie Ng, the colorectal cancer researcher who authored the database study, told Angus Chen. “That’s what motivates us to do the work, find out what might be causing this, and what unique features we could target so that we can better treat these patients. It’s something that keeps me up at night, and one of the biggest questions facing our scientific community today.”

Ng, who serves as the director of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center, discussed in a Q&A what kinds of insights the database might offer, and what her team is learning about the increasing rate of colorectal cancer in young patients.

A new series in The Lancet argues for the need to investigate a paradox of men’s health: why men experience worse health outcomes than women, even though they hold undeniable privilege. In their approach, the series authors move away from looking at men’s health as an issue of sex, broadening the frame to focus on gender. “Men’s health is defined and shaped by the culturally defined roles, responsibilities, attributes, and entitlements associated with being (or being seen as) a man, as well as power relations between and among women and men,” they write in the introduction.

A first paper proposes a framework that analyzes men’s health through an intersectional lens, focusing on structural determinants of health. A second looks at the available data about men’s life expectancy and burden of disability, trying — with limitations due to the lack of an intersectional perspective in many of the studies so far — to tease out risk factors and causes. The third paper proposes a political strategy that advances men’s health as a contributing factor to the shared public good.

Discussion of men’s health is wont to raise the question of whether it is detracting from women’s. The authors defend their choice. “A gendered approach to health is not a zero-sum game; it can serve to enhance wellbeing for all,” they write.

This week, STAT Executive Editor Rick Berke travelled to Washington, D.C., to accept in memory of Helen Branswell the Kovler Prize for Trust in Life Science Journalism at the Foundation for the National Institutes of Health dinner. It was an elegant event at Union Station, with 350 luminaries from science and health, including current and former NIH directors.

The highlight of the evening was a video that Helen recorded in late summer to accept the award. She talked about her work and a career she so deeply loved. As readers of this newsletter know, Helen has been a frequent contributor to Morning Rounds over the last 11 years, tirelessly sharing her insights on infectious disease news. (In fact, Helen’s first writings on Covid-19 appeared here.)

Heartbroken as we all are by her loss, I hope you’ll watch and come away inspired but one of the truly greats.

#5722. Post-midterms, hospitals still face a long road to policy relief, advisers warn

Post-midterms, hospitals still face a long road to policy relief, advisers warn" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hospitals facing major policy headwinds won’t be able to sustain operations through cost cutting or revenue protections alone, and they shouldn’t bank on immediate political relief following this week’s midterm results, BRG policy and health system operations consultants warn.

Health systems across the country have been gearing up for the years-long rollout of Medicare and Medicaid policy changes from 2025’s H.R. 1, whose standout changes, such as Medicaid work requirements and state-directed payment restrictions, will begin in earnest on Jan. 1. The implementation is expected to reduce the number of patients with coverage and limit supplemental payments to providers, compounding challenges they’re already facing this year after expired Affordable Care Act subsidies pushed many patients off marketplace coverage.

“I’m generally an optimist as [my] personality, but the quote that comes to me is ‘It can never be so bad that it can’t get worse,” David Wildebrandt, a managing director in BRG’s healthcare practice, said during a Thursday media roundtable on federal policy takeaways for healthcare providers. “It’s really very troubling, the cumulative toll of everything that’s happening, because health systems have an incredibly difficult ecosystem in general in terms of capacity constraints, payer mix, softer volumes.”

Those headwinds will land amid a midterm election in which healthcare issues are top items for voters. Reversing or hobbling H.R. 1 has emerged as a priority for Democratic candidates and party leaders, promises that would have no small impact on hospitals hoping for a financial lifeline.

“I do think the biggest ticket item here for the next couple of years is how One Big Beautiful Bill Act implementation goes, how states respond and whether or not Congress tries to have a say by potentially trying to amend that bill in the first couple of years,” John Barkett, managing director in BRG’s Healthcare Transactions and Strategy practice, and formerly an advisor on the White House Domestic Policy Council, said. “It's not uncommon for big bills, including Obamacare or Medicare or any other big bill, to be amended within a couple of years of passage.”

In a scenario where Democrats take both the House (currently considered very likely by pollsters) and the Senate (more of a toss-up), BRG’s healthcare practice advisors said they anticipate a slew of new congressional oversight and investigations into health agencies and some of the organizations they’d cut deals with in recent years. And even if they can’t get a partisan health bill signed into law, there’s still room to write and pass bills that could become new policy in a future majority, as was the case with Medicaid work requirements pushed by Republicans during the end of the Biden administration but ultimately codified last year.

As for the OBBBA, the BRG consultants acknowledged that revisions to the sweeping Medicaid changes are possible, but pointed out the steep hill they’d need to climb.

“President Trump will still be president, and he will view a policy that amends the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in favor of hospitals as a concession to Democrats—and therefore, he’ll be looking for something in return,” Barkett said. “And so the question will be—how big is the ask for what the Trump administration would want in return for amending a signature law … and what he’s asking for would have to be palatable for Democrats. And that’s where I think there’s a lot of uncertainty right now.”

“Providers shouldn’t really plan on relief coming from Washington in that way,” Dave Brueggeman, another managing director in BRG’s healthcare practice, said of an OBBBA amendment and a potential swift return of marketplace subsidies.

Barkett noted that second-term, lame duck presidents tend to look at their legacy as lawmaking grinds to a halt. That could make Trump and his administration “even more emboldened to take action through [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid] rulemaking,” he said.

“The question I’m thinking about is—what signals is the president giving about what he wants his legacy to be on healthcare in the last couple of years,” he said. “I’m not sure that anyone who’s saying they know what that is necessarily has the mind of the president. I think it could go in several directions, and it’s particularly interesting given that the Supreme Court … has been constricting what an executive branch can do when they’re thinking creatively about how to interpret statutes.”

Should Republicans maintain control of The Hill, Barkett said the industry should expect a continuation of the policy agenda from the past two years—reduced coverage, lower spending and deference to regulatory agencies—with “maybe some bipartisan work going on,” such as pharmacy benefit manager reforms from earlier this year.

“The bottom line here is that revenue pressure from the OBBBA isn't a one-year problem,” said Brueggeman. “It builds over the next decade, and the systems that come out of it in best shape will be the ones that start adjusting the revenue and cost strategies now.”

The policy landscape is unprecedented ground for management teams that, likely for the first time in their careers, are facing a year in which overall health insurance coverage isn't increasing.

Wildebrandt's chief advice, based on best practices BRG is seeing among big names like HCA Healthcare and Tenet Healthcare, is to cut through the unknowns and develop a financial exposure plan with “very sophisticated predictions of what's going to happen with charity care, uncompensated care, the amount of uninsured, EBITDA forecasts."

“The one thing I would certainly want to impress upon everyone is [that] it is different for every hospital. You cannot use a blanket statement,” he said of the policy impacts going into effect. Such predictions “really create a true north for everyone to look at. […] Some of the systems that are doing that, it’s been very much an awakening event.”

The immediate next priority, Wildebrandt said, is for systems to model and protect enrollment among patients who will still be eligible for coverage after January’s work requirements implementation deadline, for instance by “standing up outreach centers to help with the documentation and the education of the work requirements.” Brueggeman similarly raised red flags over yet-to-be-shared state guidance on how the changes could impact Medicaid presumptive eligibility, and noted that many BRG hospital clients are reviewing their collections and self-pay and charity care policies amid an expectation of increased payment difficulties.

From there, health systems will need to begin ramping up their cost optimization and strategic realignment, likely to a greater extent than what they’ve already pursued over the past year.

“What we share with our clients and folks that are really getting ahead of this is another 5% to 7% of cost reduction on top of what they're already doing,” he said. “And that really gets you into deeper areas beyond labor, beyond supply chain. What we're working on mostly is a transformational roadmap.”

The chief opportunities here, he said, involve integrated care models and leaning into many of the skills systems developed under risk-based arrangements to direct patients to community providers or other lower-cost settings when possible.

“We’ll likely see an explosion of growth in partnerships with FQHCs and other community organizations to get folks into the right care setting and reduce unnecessary utilization,” he said. “And another important area, one we’ve honestly given some lip service to over time, is partnering to expand ambulatory access and, again, reduce preventable hospital use.”

Wildebrandt described these efforts as requiring “structural changes” addressing “fixed costs, and not just working into variable costs.” That means taking a hard look at what’s currently on offer.

“We see many organizations assessing their portfolio, looking at service rationalization—especially big systems that have integrated and have redundant OB units within the same perimeter,” he said. “You'll see more Centers of Excellence coming out of this, which will decrease access, but consolidating services, OB, pediatric intensive care units, and other non-core programs like post-acute rehab. … You’re seeing folks also spinning things off, spinning hospitals off, spinning service lines off. So definitely a lot of activity in this space.”

Leaders from major nonprofit health systems who were on the panel agreed. Matt Brown, president of CommonSpirit Health’s South Region, said it’s become more routine to hear of cost-conscious systems targeting stiffer benchmarks for their labor spending—salary, wages and benefits expenses below 45% of patient service revenue, “when 15 years ago under 60% was appropriate."

He and Gail Kosyla, chief financial officer at AtlantiCare, also acknowledged that nonprofits are already weighing options on service lines that are losing money for the system, noting that providers could mitigate the impact on patient access by partnering with another community provider already offering the same services.

“Those are difficult decisions, and they really go to patient need, community need, as well as that financial component,” Kosyla said during the roundtable.

With the scope of headwinds to come, panelists agreed that cost management alone won't close the gap without corresponding efforts to protect revenue.

Brueggeman said his team has been working “every day” on an “explosive growth” in termination planning, as providers negotiating new network agreements with payers are increasingly willing to play chicken in order to maximize revenue. Should those disputes come to a head, a hospital’s network exit could mean reduced access to care for local patients.

Brueggeman noted that the contentious negotiations have recently lost a natural common ground. Risk-based arrangements with shared upsides and downsides have become less appealing to providers due to a “lack of ability to specifically predict what those outcomes would look like,” with the policy changes, he said. “That creates a significant tension against what was, at one time, considered an outlet in these negotiations of creating a shared responsibility around risk. It's creating a little bit of a dam in that process.”

CommonSpirit’s Brown was up front about the need to go toe-to-toe, and the benefits for doing so.

“We’re doing everything we can with payers to understand how we maximize our reimbursement,” he said. “That means draconian things at times. We’ve had markets go out of network with Medicare Advantage providers. And we’ve gotten back in recently—specifically a community in Texas. We went out for a while and then came back in as a national player.”

“We have to do everything we can to leverage our scale in negotiations with payers—and with states to ensure that we don't get hit with provider fee problems in places like Kentucky, Colorado and California to the level that H.R. 1 projects,” he added.

#5721. EXCLUSIVE: ‘Members Only: Palm Beach’ Star Hilary Musser Reveals Plans for New Show With a Possible Real Estate Twist

“Members Only: Palm Beach” star Hilary Musser is working on a new TV project that could incorporate the area’s luxury real estate—and says she would also serve as a producer.

While the future of the Netflix hit remains uncertain, Musser says she is already pursuing another opportunity, with casting among the steps she is working on.

“I’m working on a different show right now,” she says. It's a project “where I would also be a producer.”

Musser is keeping most of the details private for now. She says the network has not been determined, but the Palm Beach County setting could provide an opening to feature the industry in which she has built her business.

“In Palm Beach County, we’re famous for our real estate,” she says.

However, she does not envision creating a series focused entirely on property. Instead, she says real estate could be one element of a broader concept.

The project comes as Musser considers what she wants to do following her appearance on “Members Only: Palm Beach.” The series has not been canceled nor renewed.

“It doesn’t really matter to me if the show gets renewed,” she says.

Her introduction to that series came through fellow cast member Taja Abitbol, whom she met while serving on a fundraising committee.

During a cocktail party, Abitbol asked whether she would be interested in interviewing for a TV show about country club life in Palm Beach.

Musser agreed, having previously passed on other opportunities to appear on camera.

She says she was approached about a Palm Beach housewives show in 2005, but declined after being filmed because she worried about the potential impact on her marriage and young son.

This time, she decided to embrace the opportunity.

During filming, Musser says she did not prepare dialogue or attempt to adopt a different personality. With a real estate business to consider, she wanted to present herself as she normally would.

“I didn’t prepare what I was going to say,” she says.

Alongside her TV appearance, Musser was also working on a waterfront spec home that she says was completed in June and is now offered for $42.5 million.

The property is a development she built to sell. Separately, she describes her personal home as smaller but similarly finished.

According to Musser, the spec home sits along the Intracoastal Waterway, across from the Palm Beach property being developed by billionaire Ken Griffin.

Inside, she says the emphasis is on distinctive finishes and an uncompromising approach to quality, with leather-wrapped refrigerator handles, leather-lined kitchen drawers, Italian marble, and a separate chef’s kitchen.

For Musser, those details reflect what she believes wealthy buyers want: a property that offers something different from other luxury homes, with spaces that provide their own reasons to stay in.

She describes a dining room that forms part of the wine room, along with a kitchen, living room, and theater that each deliver a different experience.

“Every room is a destination,” she says. “A place where you can go and enjoy your friends and your family.”

Her own lifestyle helps guide those decisions. Rather than approaching a development solely as something to sell, she considers whether she would enjoy living there herself.

“And I build every house as if I’m going to live in it,” she says.

Musser initially obtained her real estate license to improve her access to properties for her development business.

She felt desirable opportunities were being claimed before reaching the market and wanted to put herself in a better position to find them.

After working with a friend for a couple of years, she earned her broker’s license. Representing clients was not originally the goal, but requests from people in her community led her to begin showing and listing homes.

She says her real estate business’ gross revenue quadrupled last year, and she regards her TV experience as a success from a business perspective.

Now, she is also pursuing brand partnerships, merchandising, social media opportunities, and a book she says she had wanted to work on since before the COVID-19 pandemic.

“The show has just opened up some new doors for me,” she says.

Still, the work behind her property business remains far less glamorous than the waterfront homes might suggest. Musser points to negotiating contracts, preparing properties for showings, following up with agents, and waiting for the right buyer.

“You wish you could just produce a buyer when you want one,” she says. “But it doesn’t work like that.”

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.
