#5681. What Each Party Promises on Housing Affordability as Congress Hangs in the Balance

As they jockey for control of Congress in a tight midterm race, Democrats and Republicans have each made promises that their party will focus on housing affordability.

Both parties have spent the year pushing messages about affordability, especially in housing. Homeowners are being hammered with higher insurance and property tax rates. Higher interest rates have frozen the housing market. And young people are overwhelmingly concerned about whether they'll ever own a home at all. With many close races, control of Congress could hinge on these concerns.

Then there's the issue of how to implement laws Congress has already passed. The bipartisan 21st Century Road to Housing Act promises reforms in dozens of provisions aimed at cutting red tape and encouraging the construction of more homes. Congress will oversee the rollout of those new programs while also working with the final two years of the Trump administration—and the market will be looking to Washington for clarity.

Jeff Holzmann, COO of Dallas-based real estate firm RREAF, tells Realtor.com® the industry needs clear rules to make long-term investment decisions. Broad rules such as the new ban on institutional investors in the housing market require clarity or else they might not achieve the affordability Congress intended with the bill.

"From my operator's perspective, the bigger question is whether these regulations will continue to encourage private capital to invest in building new homes and improving existing ones, as that's what drives our business," Holzmann says. "If that pans out, I believe it can make a real difference in affordability over time."

Over the course of the year, many Republicans have said they want to see reforms to the housing finance system. These rules, they've said, have discouraged banks and financial institutions from infusing money into the housing market.

House Financial Services Committee Chair Rep. French Hill (R-AR) told the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in September that he wanted to see reforms to the BASEL III framework, aimed to encourage more banks to finance mortgages and construction loans.

"That should take steps to encourage the large banks to participate in the secondary market for housing," Hill said. "I think Dodd-Frank went too far on this point. Essentially, by the capital standards for a construction loan, pushed a lot of the biggest banks out of that business. It also limited mortgage servicing rights by the large financial institutions. Both of those things, at the margin, raise the cost of liquidity for housing."

Rep. Mike Flood (R-NE), who chairs the Housing and Insurance Subcommittee, said in July he wants to see single-family homebuilding exempted from the prevailing wage requirements in the Davis-Bacon and Related Acts.

Flood and Hill have both said they want to exempt homebuilding materials from the Build America Buy America Act. That adds sourcing requirements to many building materials that drive up their costs.

At the same time, Republicans have also backed the Trump administration's shift of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development away from "housing first" homelessness programs. HUD has repeatedly criticized what Secretary Scott Turner calls a "homeless industrial complex." In alternate, HUD has pursued programs that emphasize treatment and recovery. But it's clashed with states and service providers and pursued "diversity equity and inclusion" programs as well.

Democrats have called for additional spending to help bolster a variety of housing programs, especially those regarding tenant and homeowner protections.

Earlier this year, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) said Democrats would pursue laws cracking down on junk fees and on predatory companies abusing tenants and using price-fixing algorithms.

A number of Democrat-led bills this year have also proposed expanding funding for Section 8 vouchers, rent relief, programs to help curtail evictions, and expansion of the Low-Income Tax Credit, which produces about 40,000 to 50,000 units a year of affordable housing.

Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO), ranking member of the Banking subcommittee, told the Chamber of Commerce in September that both parties must be focused on effective compromise.

"We're woefully lacking in legislation that can move through both the House and the Senate and get to the president's desk," he said.

Democrats are also likely to resume efforts for stricter data center regulation. They sank a Republican-led bill that encouraged utilities to shield ratepayers from data center costs in favor of a proposal with more stringent enforcement powers for the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

The party will also have to contend with a wave of Democratic Socialist candidates elected at the local and state level. Those candidates have shown different levels of support for policies like rent control and "housing for all."

The 43-member bipartisan Build America Caucus put out a 95-page primer for issues it would pursue regardless of who is in control of either chamber next year.

Its housing agenda includes fast-tracking residential construction in areas where cities have "outdated" zoning constraints in place. It also wants to see programs that encourage housing near transit and under-used federal land, as well as modernization of building code standards.

“The problem isn't a lack of good ideas; it's the bureaucratic red tape slowing projects down for years," Rep. Sharice Davids (D-KS) said in a statement with the primer.

Democrats and Republicans in Congress have found common ground in some parts of the housing debate. For instance, the More Homes on the Market Act, which would double the capital gains tax exclusion, has attracted over 170 co-sponsors in the House and Senate.

Both parties have pitched changes to the capital gains tax scheme using different methods, but none advanced this year.

Democrats and Republicans have also routinely put forth a few bills aimed at promoting housing innovations and designs. For instance, last week, Reps. Maggie Goodlander (D-NH) and Jefferson Shreve (R-IN) put forth a bill that would encourage pre-reviewed, permit-ready home designs. They said in a joint statement they hope it would mean faster approvals.

"I’m working with Republicans and Democrats to clear away every rule that makes it slower and more expensive to build a home in New Hampshire," Goodlander said.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5680. The surprisingly simple exercise that could lower your blood pressure

New research suggests that exercising just once or twice a week may be enough to maintain some of the blood pressure benefits gained from regular physical activity, at least over a short period. However, people who continue exercising three times weekly may experience larger and more sustained improvements.

The findings, published in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine, suggest that even a single weekly session of isometric exercise could help people preserve improvements in blood pressure when they cannot commit to a more frequent workout schedule.

Isometric exercise involves tightening muscles while holding the body in a fixed position for several minutes. Common examples include wall squats, planks, and handgrip exercises.

Earlier research has found that isometric training can lower blood pressure more effectively than other types of exercise, sometimes producing reductions comparable to or greater than those achieved with certain medications. However, researchers have not fully understood how often these exercises need to be performed to maintain their cardiovascular benefits.

To investigate, researchers enrolled 100 adults whose average age was 37.4 years. Participants had systolic blood pressure ranging from normal to high-normal levels (120-140 mmHg) and did not regularly participate in structured exercise programs.

Under expert guidelines, systolic blood pressure between 130 and 139 mmHg falls into the "high-normal" category, which warrants specific lifestyle recommendations from healthcare professionals. None of the participants had been diagnosed with hypertension.

To qualify, volunteers had to be free of injuries and illnesses, have no current or previous use of blood pressure medication, and be nonsmokers. They also had to consume no more than 14 units of alcohol per week.

Participants were randomly assigned to five groups. One served as a control group, while the other four began the same four-week exercise program at home, focusing on isometric movements involving the lower body.

The training consisted of four wall squat holds per session, with two minutes of seated recovery between each hold. Participants completed this routine three times weekly during the first four weeks.

After this initial training period, the four exercise groups followed different schedules for another four weeks. One continued with three weekly sessions, another reduced its frequency to twice weekly, and a third performed the exercises only once a week. The fourth group stopped training altogether.

Researchers evaluated blood pressure, heart rate, and additional measures of cardiovascular function at the beginning of the experiment and again after four and eight weeks.

Even One Weekly Workout Helped Preserve Blood Pressure Benefits

After the first four weeks, all four exercise groups showed significant improvements compared with the control group. These included reductions in systolic blood pressure, which measures pressure when the heart contracts, and diastolic blood pressure, which measures pressure when the heart relaxes. Mean arterial pressure, a measure of average blood pressure throughout the cardiac cycle, also decreased significantly.

These initial results were consistent with earlier studies demonstrating the blood pressure benefits of isometric exercise. However, after participants switched to their assigned maintenance schedules, the groups no longer showed statistically significant differences in diastolic blood pressure.

By the end of the eight-week study, participants exercising just once or twice weekly had maintained significant reductions in systolic blood pressure and mean arterial pressure compared with the control group. Neither schedule maintained a statistically significant improvement in diastolic blood pressure.

The greatest benefits appeared among participants who continued performing wall squats three times per week. Their systolic blood pressure fell by an average of 13.73 mmHg (-13.73 mmHg) from the beginning of the study.

By comparison, the twice-weekly group experienced an average reduction of 6.95 mmHg, while participants exercising once a week recorded a decrease of 6.56 mmHg.

Those who maintained the three-session schedule also preserved improvements in other cardiovascular measurements, including total peripheral resistance (an indication that blood vessels have narrowed) and heart rate variability.

Stopping Exercise Caused Blood Pressure Benefits to Fade

The results also revealed what happened when participants stopped exercising completely.

Those who discontinued wall squats after the initial four weeks experienced a reversal of their earlier blood pressure improvements. By the end of the study, their readings were no longer statistically different from those of the control group.

This finding suggests that maintaining some level of regular isometric exercise may be important for preserving the cardiovascular improvements gained during training.

However, the researchers emphasized that the maintenance phase lasted only four weeks. Additional studies following participants for longer periods will be needed to determine whether less frequent training can preserve these benefits over months or years.

"The study demonstrates that while lower frequency isometric exercise training may be sufficient to maintain blood pressure reductions over the short term, higher frequencies are required to preserve these benefits and the associated vascular and cardiac autonomic adaptations," the researchers write.

"The study offers evidence that lower frequency isometric exercise training can help maintain short-term blood pressure reductions, providing a pragmatic option for individuals with limited time or adherence challenges."

#5676. Real Estate or Stocks? Risk Tolerance, Markets Key Most Decisions

There’s always been a question about which is the better investment long term, real estate or stocks? Opinions vary, but there is one thing for sure: You can’t reside in your stock portfolio. Another thing for sure is if you ask real estate pros for opinions, you pretty much get the same answer.

Those willing to accept a fair amount of risk will likely do better in the stock market over time. The 10-year annual S&P 500 performance breakdown from 2016 to 2025 wins hands down, or palms up if collecting profits. Within that decade were four gains in the mid-20% range, with only two negative return years. Of course, what happened in the past has no bearing on the future.

Real estate properties have historically increased in value over time. In 1970, the average price of an American house was $27,000. A comparable investment property now would be worth approximately $500,000, according to Federal Reserve Economic Data. That appreciation could represent a meaningful source of retirement funding if the property were eventually sold.

According to the Zillow Home Value Index, the average United States home value is $366,157, up 1.2% over the past year, and homes go to pending in around 27 days. Stock returns can be volatile due to several factors. Economic events such as recessions, interest-rate fluctuations and geopolitical tensions can significantly impact stock prices. Few would probably be shocked if the continuing war with Iran cratered the stock market at some point.

Stocks now account for more than a 30% share of total U.S. household assets, versus real estate at closer to 25%, according to TD Securities. That wasn’t always so. In the mid-2000s, real estate represented more than 30% of total household wealth, while stocks were around 15%.

So what would you as a real estate pro tell clients if the stocks vs. real estate subject arose?

“Your first investment property is the home you live in,” asserts Pam Rosser Thistle, with Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Fox & Roach, Realtors® in Philadelphia, while admitting the stock market numbers win right now. “Over time, it appreciates. And you enjoy it. Win, win! Right now I am bullish on happiness, and owning a home is part of that. Appreciation is not like it was during COVID. But over time, your home will make you money when you sell in most cases as long as you stay in it for five to seven-plus years.”

Josh Jarboe, principal broker/owner of RE/MAX Empire in Mount Washington, Kentucky, has never believed real estate should be viewed as a guaranteed investment. But he firmly believes it remains one of the strongest, proven paths for long-term wealth creation.

“Unlike the stock market, homeownership offers something beyond financial returns: stability, utility, leverage and the opportunity to build equity while enjoying the asset itself. Higher home prices and mortgage rates have undoubtedly changed the equation, especially for first-time buyers. However, I remind clients that real estate and stocks aren’t necessarily competing investments. They serve different purposes, and a well-diversified financial strategy can include both.”

Leslie Hirsch, a broker at Christie’s International Real Estate New York, admits that many of her clients have been questioning whether to keep their money invested in the stock market, which has been performing so well, or purchase real estate.

“In New York City, this is driving a very strong rental market, with record prices being paid, as would-be buyers opt to rent instead of tying up cash in real estate,” she says. “Financial advisors/portfolio managers are encouraging clients to stay in the market and not buy real estate. On the flip side, there is chatter about the stock market being too good to last. People need housing, and they also want to diversify investments, maximize returns and mitigate risk.”

Hirsch tailors her advice depending on a client’s personal situation, but admits that generally speaking, the anticipated timeline to hold onto property and see appreciation has shifted.

“I cannot tell someone that we would expect to see ‘x’ amount of appreciation per year, as we have not seen predictable appreciation in Manhattan for 10-plus years,” she says. “Instead of a five-year property value growth cycle, we are now seeing 10-year-plus cycles, and the key is to buy property during the down cycle and sell when it’s up.

“For clients that I know plan to move cities, expand their family or upgrade in three to five years, I try to manage expectations and sometimes suggest they look at renting instead of buying while saving up for the bigger purchase down the road. Some people who would only ever consider being homeowners (never renters) will now consider it.”

Hirsch knows that housing is a fundamental need, and thus is not worried about mortgage rates and the market because the market will ultimately adjust to meet the climate of the day.

“If housing prices become unaffordable, then prices will come down,” she explains. “If the rents go too high, then purchasing becomes the better option again. What I do worry about is the affordability of housing for first-time homebuyers and people starting out in their careers.

“The second home market is where I see even more dramatic fluctuation happening because that is a ‘want’ and not a ‘need.’ When we see home values decrease enough, we eventually see investor buyers swoop in to purchase them. Then, when the stock market stops performing as well, we will see people pivoting back to real estate again, and the prices will stabilize.”

Jarrod Duncan, also with Christie’s International Real Estate New York, has a take as a real estate investor, feeling that while stocks may be booming, real estate is still a strong long-term investment.

“I own many properties in the Southeast that have increased in value exponentially since purchasing them,” he says. “I am also invested in the stock market, as I feel like it’s important to have multiple vehicles for wealth building. I do agree that the stock market has been a good place to be the last few years. So has real estate in certain places, especially in the Southeast, where people are moving for tax advantages, etc.

“I also think that investing in real estate can be even better in an elevated rate environment. Higher rates keep prices down, and you can always refinance, but an attractive deal may not come around again for years. There are some potential tax advantages to investing in real estate, such as the ability to take advantage of accelerated depreciation and ongoing costs to offset other sources of income. I remain committed to investing in real estate and recommend it to others if the fit is right for their long-term goals.”

Jarboe echoes the sentiment that the concern isn’t people choosing stocks over real estate, but the growing number of Americans being priced out of homeownership altogether.

“The longer affordability remains a challenge, the greater the potential wealth gap between those who own real estate and those who don’t,” he says. “Ultimately, I encourage clients to focus less on timing the market and more on whether purchasing a home aligns with their financial position, lifestyle and long-term goals. Real estate isn’t a guaranteed investment, especially in ‘boom-towns/cities’, but historically, patience and responsible ownership have rewarded those who take the long view.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5675. Behind Charleston’s Most Famous Gates: The Sword Gate House Asks a Record $35 Million

Some of the most iconic ironwork in Charleston, SC, guards the entrance to a home that’s undergone a complete renovation in the six years since it last changed hands.

The Sword Gate House, at 32 Legare Street is on the market for $35 million, a record-setting ask for Charleston. The estate last sold in 2020 for $10 million.

The house dates to the early 1800s and takes its name from the sword-and-spear gates forged by local ironworker Christopher Werner. British consul George Hopley installed them around 1850, and they’ve drawn crowds of sightseers ever since.

Over two centuries, the property has served as a private residence, a private school, an inn and a vacation retreat. Among its past owners was Jessie Lincoln Randolph, Abraham Lincoln’s granddaughter, who bought it in the 1930s.

The schoolhouse chapter still shapes the property with its towering perimeter walls dating to the 19th century, when the home housed a girls’ academy.

The compound totals 17,142 square feet on roughly 0.87 acre, one of the largest residential lots downtown. The main house holds eight bedrooms, each with its own bathroom, plus two powder rooms.

“The current owners spared no expense and touched every surface of the property, both inside and out,” says Turner. The interiors, which are a true feast for the eyes, were created by designer Cortney Bishop.

When the owners bought the home, its only kitchen was a catering setup on the ground floor. They combined two main-level rooms into a new kitchen and informal dining space with a wood-burning fireplace and a piazza for dining outdoors. The original kitchen stayed in place for caterers and staff, “so the main living level can be party-perfect,” says Turner.

The ballroom remains the estate’s centerpiece, with gilded crown molding and a carved mantel. A custom magnolia chandelier hangs in the curved grand staircase, a nod to the centuries-old magnolia that shades the home’s triple piazzas.

The primary suite stretches across the south side of the second floor, with a soaking tub set before a fireplace, two water closets and a dressing room that Turner says “rivals a stylish boutique.”

Outside, the owners added a heated and cooled pool, a fireside dining area and a linear fountain anchored by a glass conservatory. “This fountain has even been topped with a dining table for an unforgettable celebration under the stars,” Turner says.

As if the main house renovation wasn't enough, a stunning two-story carriage house adds three guest suites, including one with a full kitchen. Two gated driveways and a two-car garage round out the property.

The estate is also a short walk from King Street’s shops and galleries.

“For today’s luxury buyer, time is the ultimate luxury,” she says. “All the hard work of design, restoration, renovation, and investment have already been completed.”

#5674. A simple liquid can stop cavities without drilling, major study confirms

A cavity doesn't always have to mean drilling, injections, or an uncomfortable visit to the dentist. A major clinical trial has confirmed that a simple, inexpensive liquid can stop tooth decay in young children, potentially preventing painful infections and the need for dental surgery.

The treatment, called silver diamine fluoride (SDF), takes only seconds to apply to each affected tooth. Rather than removing damaged tooth material and placing a filling, a dentist uses a tiny sponge tipped applicator to paint the liquid directly onto the cavity. The process requires no drilling, injections, or sedation.

The findings could have enormous implications for childhood dental care. Every year, thousands of young children in the United States visit emergency departments because of untreated cavities. Emergency physicians generally cannot provide the dental procedures needed to address the underlying problem, leaving some children with ongoing pain and infections. Others ultimately need dental surgery under general anesthesia, which makes them completely unconscious during the procedure.

Now, researchers led by the University of Michigan have produced compelling evidence that a much simpler approach can stop many cavities from getting worse.

Major Clinical Trial Confirms Silver Diamine Fluoride Works

Published in JAMA Pediatrics, the Phase III clinical trial included 830 children younger than 6. Participants were recruited through dental clinics, pediatric medical practices, and Head Start and Early Head Start programs in Michigan, New York, and Iowa.

Head Start and Early Head Start are federally supported programs that provide early childhood education and related services to eligible families.

The results showed that a solution containing 38% silver diamine fluoride successfully stopped decay in more than half of the affected baby teeth when treatment was provided at six month intervals.

Dentists refer to this as arresting tooth decay, meaning the damaged area stops deteriorating. Unlike a traditional filling, the treatment does not replace lost tooth structure. Instead, it helps prevent existing decay from progressing.

SDF works through the combined effects of silver and fluoride. Silver helps combat bacteria associated with tooth decay, while fluoride helps strengthen the mineral structure of teeth and resist further damage.

"This is a very effective and safe treatment -- even in children as young as 1," said Margherita Fontana, professor of dentistry at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry and the study's lead investigator.

A Simple Treatment Could Help Millions Avoid Dental Pain

Tooth decay is the most common chronic disease among children, affecting more than 40% of American children. Although cavities may initially cause few noticeable symptoms, untreated decay can eventually lead to severe toothaches, infections, problems eating and sleeping, missed school days, and repeated medical appointments.

For young children, conventional dental treatment can also be particularly challenging. Some are too young to remain still throughout a procedure, while others experience significant fear or anxiety.

SDF offers an alternative for many of these patients because it can be applied quickly without the equipment and procedures required for a traditional filling.

Fontana said the benefits could extend well beyond young children. Older adults, people with developmental or physical disabilities, individuals with severe dental anxiety, and patients who have difficulty obtaining conventional dental care could also benefit.

There is, however, one important tradeoff. SDF permanently turns the decayed portion of a treated tooth dark, which can be especially noticeable on front teeth. The discoloration is primarily cosmetic, but it may influence whether patients and families choose the treatment.

For many people, avoiding pain, drilling, or more invasive procedures may outweigh that drawback.

Why This Decades-Old Treatment Could Soon Reach More Patients

Silver diamine fluoride is not a newly invented substance. Dentists have successfully used it to manage cavities in numerous countries for decades.

In the United States, the FDA approved SDF as a medical device for treating tooth sensitivity in 2014. Dentists have also used it off-label to stop cavities, meaning they apply an authorized product for a purpose beyond its original approved indication.

What has been missing is large-scale clinical evidence from U.S. populations establishing its safety and effectiveness for treating tooth decay, a key step toward obtaining FDA approval for that specific use.

The University of Michigan trial was designed to help fill that gap.

"If we want more children and families to benefit from this treatment, we need rigorous evidence showing both that it works and that it's safe. From a public health perspective, if we want broader implementation across the United States, including in medical settings, we need carefully collected data in U.S. populations, and we now have that," Fontana said.

The investigation began in 2018 and continued despite the major disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The researchers believe stronger clinical evidence could make SDF more widely available, including in pediatric medical settings where children often receive care long before their first dental appointment.

"In medicine, clinicians want high-quality evidence before changing practice," Fontana said. "It is important to have data they can refer to because young children often see pediatricians years before they ever visit a dentist, broader acceptance could allow many more cavities to be treated while a referral to a dental home is successful, and before they become painful, infected or require surgery."

A dental home refers to an ongoing relationship with a dental care provider who can deliver preventive care, treatment, and follow-up services.

Expanding access to SDF could allow more children to receive early intervention before relatively manageable cavities develop into serious dental problems.

FDA Approval Could Expand Access to Cavity Treatment

The trial brought together researchers from the University of Michigan, New York University, the University of Iowa, and Indiana University. The National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, part of the National Institutes of Health, provided more than $12 million in funding.

The product tested was Advantage Arrest 38% SDF, supplied by Elevate Oral Care.

The findings provide clinical trial evidence that the manufacturer can use in an application seeking FDA approval of SDF as a drug for arresting dental caries, the medical term for tooth decay.

Amr Moursi, a professor of pediatric dentistry at New York University College of Dentistry and a co-principal investigator, emphasized the potential importance of that regulatory change.

"Our results support FDA approval of SDF for managing arrest of tooth decay in young children. Removing SDF from off-label status would be an important innovation which could lead to increased utilization by providers, enhanced payments by insurers and more consistent product quality," said Moursi, a co-principal investigator on the study.

For some children, receiving another application of SDF every few months could be sufficient to keep a cavity under control until the affected baby tooth naturally falls out.

Adults could also benefit, either by using SDF to manage decay over a longer period or as a temporary solution until a filling or another restorative procedure becomes affordable or practical.

The treatment is not suitable for every cavity, and stopping decay does not necessarily eliminate the need for future dental work. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that a procedure requiring only seconds to perform could help many patients avoid more complicated treatment.

"For almost anyone, this can arrest the decay and stop the infection and the pain it causes," Fontana said. "This could benefit many people."

Materials provided by University of Michigan. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5672. The secret to slower aging may be hiding in your gut

Scientists have uncovered a surprising connection between the bacteria living in the human gut and the speed at which the body ages. Researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa found that certain gut microbes are associated with slower biological aging, while others are linked to faster aging.

The study, published in Scientific Reports, found that differences in gut bacterial communities accounted for approximately 15% of the variation in participants' biological aging rates. The results suggest that the gut microbiome, the vast community of microorganisms living in the digestive system, may provide valuable clues about aging at the molecular level.

"This study advances our understanding of the relationship between the gut microbiome and biological aging," said senior author Alika K. Maunakea of the UH Mānoa John A. Burns School of Medicine. "We found that microbial patterns in the gut were significantly associated with molecular measures of aging, even independent of chronological age. These findings open important new directions for understanding how modifiable biological systems influence long-term health trajectories and longevity."

Scientists Identify Gut Bacteria Linked to Faster and Slower Aging

To investigate the relationship between gut bacteria and aging, researchers examined stool and blood samples collected from 123 adults across a wide range of ages. They identified the bacteria present in each participant's gut and compared those findings with blood-based molecular markers used to estimate the body's rate of aging.

These biological measurements differ from chronological age, which simply reflects how many years someone has been alive. Instead, they are designed to assess how quickly aging-related changes are occurring within the body.

The researchers found a notable association between the composition of the gut microbiome and DunedinPACE, an advanced biomarker that measures the pace of biological aging.

Some bacterial species stood out for their particularly strong relationships with aging. Bifidobacterium adolescentis was among the microbes most strongly associated with slower biological aging. In contrast, Succinivibrio dextrinosolvens showed one of the strongest associations with faster aging.

These differences suggest that particular patterns of gut bacteria may offer important information about how rapidly the body is aging.

How Diet, Lifestyle, and Environment May Influence Gut Health

Lead author Braden P. Kunihiro said the discovery adds to growing evidence that the gut microbiome could play an important role in precision health research, which aims to better understand individual differences in health and disease.

Unlike chronological age, the composition of the gut microbiome can change in response to everyday influences, including diet, lifestyle, and environmental conditions. This makes it a particularly interesting area of investigation for scientists studying healthy aging.

"The gut microbiome is highly responsive to lifestyle, diet, environment and other everyday exposures," Kunihiro said. "Our findings suggest that the microbiome may reflect important aspects of biological resilience and aging in ways that could eventually help inform future wellness and healthy aging strategies."

The research also included Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander participants, groups that have historically received limited representation in studies of aging and gut microorganisms.

Co-author Ruben Juarez explained that including these populations could help scientists investigate how social circumstances and environmental conditions leave lasting biological effects over the course of a person's life.

"The microbiome exists at the intersection of behavior, environment and human biology," Juarez said. "Studies like this help illuminate potential pathways through which lived experiences and social factors influence long-term health outcomes."

Could Changing Gut Bacteria Influence How We Age?

Although the findings reveal a meaningful relationship between gut bacteria and biological aging, researchers stress that the study does not establish cause and effect. In other words, finding certain microbes in people who age more slowly does not necessarily mean those bacteria are responsible for slowing the aging process.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether deliberately changing the gut microbiome can influence biological aging or improve long-term health.

Still, the findings offer a promising starting point for exploring how the microorganisms living inside us relate to the aging process and whether they could eventually help guide more personalized approaches to healthy aging.

"This is an important early step toward understanding the gut microbiome's relationship with healthy aging," Maunakea said. "Future research will help clarify the mechanisms involved and whether these microbial signatures may eventually contribute to precision approaches for promoting long-term health and wellness."

#5671. This 138-Year-Old Los Angeles ‘Unicorn’ House Is Completely Drenched in Purple—and Listed for $2 Million

A house drenched in purple and set on a hill in Los Angeles, CA offers a window into the past.

“I kind of call it a unicorn. Los Angeles doesn't have a lot of 138-year-old houses anymore,” says listing agent Laurie Turner with Coldwell Banker Residential Brokerage – Pasadena. “Los Angeles was a big agricultural zone, and people were coming out west for opportunity and land and things that they didn't have on the East Coast and in the Midwest.”

The Queen Anne Victorian on about half an acre was built in 1888 and is listed for $2 million.

“I just love it. It’s such a happy place to be and it's warm and inviting… and although a little dilapidated right now, you can see what it was when Leonora was living there.”

Leonora Pierotti Thomas bought the place in 1979, and her estate is selling it.

“She was an eccentric artist, never married, [who] had the wherewithal to have a home like this, travel the world, entertain,” Turner says. “I've heard stories. I unfortunately never had the opportunity to meet her, but she just sounds like a kick.”

“It was yellow when Leonora bought it and from what I hear from her cousin, everything about [Leonora] was purple,” Turner explains. “She drove a purple Hummer. The garden hoses were purple. I have a picture that was sent out in memory [of her], and she is with her poodle and she had dyed her poodle’s fur purple.”

The color is prevalent both inside and outside the house and even extends to the newish roof with its purple accents.

The 2,700-square-foot house has four bedrooms and three bathrooms and both the kitchen and primary suite are part of an addition in the past decade. It’s no surprise the kitchen island, some lighting, and several walls are purple.

Everything needs a bit of work. Some of the plaster is coming off the walls, but everything in the house, including the pool, is in working condition.

“I'm calling it a historic restoration project versus a fixer because fixer sounds like a fix and flip,” Turner explains, adding a contractor she consulted said it would cost at least a million dollars to restore it.

“I'm really looking [for a buyer] who has the vision and the wherewithal to update the home, bring it back to its glory, live in it, and do right by the neighbors and the neighborhood.”

Known as Esperanza House, the home stood on the hill before the streetcar even reached the area.

“[My favorite thing about the house] is the approach as you come up Mount Royal and you see the facade and then the driveway comes up. You wrap around the house, and you see the turret there on the front and the colors in the roof and the filigree across the top of the roof line,” Turner says. “It's a nod to the past and it's my job to find the next steward to keep the chapter going.”

#5670. Washington state resident dies from bird flu following exposure to infected cattle

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

NEW YORK — A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such U.S. death in a year.

The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized. The person died Sunday, county health officials said.

Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5.

Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the person was infected with H5N1.

County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds recently have tested positive for H5N1.

They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms.

The H5N1 bird flu has been spreading widely among wild birds, poultry, cows and other animals for several years. Health concerns escalated in early 2024 when infections spread among U.S. livestock. Its presence in the environment increases the chances that people will be exposed, and potentially catch it, officials have said.

More than 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since the beginning of 2024, according to the CDC. But there is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says.

The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday.

Officials continue to urge people who have contact with sick or dead birds to take precautions, including wearing respiratory and eye protection and gloves when handling poultry. People who work on farms are considered to be at higher risk.

#5669. Low testosterone may make sugar far more harmful to your liver

Low testosterone can contribute to several health problems, and an unhealthy diet may make some of those risks even worse. One major concern is metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), a condition that affects approximately 40% of adult men worldwide and has become a significant global health issue.

Fatty liver, the earliest stage of MASLD, occurs when excess fat builds up in the liver. Several factors are associated with the condition, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, low testosterone levels, and excessive fructose consumption from sugary drinks and processed foods. However, scientists have not fully understood how these factors interact or whether their combined effects are more harmful than each one individually.

How Low Testosterone and Fructose Affect the Liver

To investigate this connection, a research team from the Graduate School of Agriculture, led by graduate student Hiroki Takahashi and Associate Professor Naoki Harada, examined how reduced testosterone and high fructose intake influence liver health.

The researchers used eight-week-old male mice and divided them into six experimental groups. Some underwent castration to lower testosterone levels, while others received a sham operation. The groups included Sham/Control, Sham/Fructose, Sham/Fructose + Antibiotics, Castration/Control, Castration/Fructose, and Castration/Fructose + Antibiotics.

To determine how these conditions affected the animals, the team analyzed liver cells and tissues, blood plasma, organic acids from the cecum, and samples of gut bacteria.

The results revealed that mice with reduced testosterone levels developed heavier livers when they consumed fructose. However, this increase in liver weight was smaller in mice that also received antibiotics.

When examined separately, low testosterone and fructose intake produced only modest changes in liver triglyceride levels. When combined, however, the two factors had a much stronger effect, significantly increasing fat accumulation and worsening fatty liver.

The researchers also identified changes in the composition of gut bacteria, altered liver gene activity, and elevated levels of pyruvate in the cecum among mice exposed to both reduced testosterone and fructose.

These findings suggested that the gut microbiome could play an important role in explaining why the combination was particularly harmful.

Further experiments helped the researchers identify a possible biological explanation for the increased liver fat.

"Upon examining this mechanism, we found that changes in the gut microbiota led to increased levels of pyruvate within the intestine. Furthermore, experiments using mouse-derived primary hepatocytes revealed that pyruvate acts synergistically with fructose to promote neutral lipid accumulation in hepatocytes," explained Takahashi.

In other words, changes in gut bacteria appeared to increase intestinal pyruvate, a compound involved in energy metabolism. Laboratory experiments with liver cells isolated from mice showed that pyruvate and fructose worked together to increase fat storage in those cells.

The discovery suggests that interactions among testosterone levels, dietary fructose, and gut bacteria may help explain how fatty liver develops and worsens.

Potential New Ways to Prevent Fatty Liver Disease

Understanding this relationship could eventually help researchers identify new approaches to preventing or treating fatty liver disease. In particular, targeting the processes through which pyruvate contributes to fat accumulation may offer promising possibilities.

"Going forward, we hope to clarify the mechanism by which pyruvate promotes triglyceride accumulation to pioneer the development of therapeutic drugs and establishment of preventive methods through dietary interventions," added Professor Harada.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and isolated mouse liver cells, they provide new insight into how hormonal changes and diet may interact to influence liver health.

The study was published in American Journal of Physiology-Endocrinology and Metabolism.

#5665. Scientists discover a hidden reason why muscles weaken with age

Muscles naturally become weaker as we get older, but scientists have discovered that some of the changes associated with aging may actually help protect muscle cells from damage. New research reveals why aging muscles shift toward a different type of muscle fiber and identifies a crucial molecule that could offer a new approach to treating muscle loss.

Muscle tissue contains bundles of fibers with different functions. Fast-twitch fibers produce powerful, rapid movements but fatigue relatively quickly. Slow-twitch fibers, by contrast, support sustained activity and contain higher concentrations of mitochondria, the cellular structures responsible for producing much of the energy muscles need.

As people age, muscle strength declines and mitochondria become less efficient. Surprisingly, aging muscles also develop a greater proportion of slow-twitch fibers, even though these fibers depend heavily on the very mitochondria that are losing their ability to function. Researchers have observed similar changes in several conditions that cause muscle wasting.

This raises an important question: Why would muscles increasingly rely on an energy-producing system that is becoming less effective?

A Crucial Molecule Linked to Muscle Aging

To investigate this puzzle, scientists focused on cardiolipin, a specialized fat molecule located almost exclusively within the inner membrane of mitochondria. Cardiolipin helps maintain the membrane's distinctive folded architecture, which is essential for proper mitochondrial activity.

When cardiolipin is lacking, mitochondria struggle to generate sufficient energy. They also become less capable of producing the chemical signals and essential materials that cells require to function.

The researchers discovered that cardiolipin levels decrease in muscle mitochondria from both mice and humans as they age or experience disease. This decline was accompanied by structural abnormalities in the mitochondria and a loss of normal function.

To determine whether reduced cardiolipin directly contributes to these changes, rather than simply occurring alongside them, the team experimentally lowered cardiolipin levels in young mice.

The results closely resembled what happens during natural aging. Muscle fibers shifted away from the fast-twitch type toward slow-twitch fibers, matching the pattern previously observed in older mice and humans.

Even more strikingly, restoring cardiolipin to approximately two-thirds of its normal concentration began reversing muscle wasting and completely prevented the premature deaths seen in the affected animals.

Why Aging Muscles Sacrifice Strength for Protection

Further experiments revealed an unexpected explanation for the transformation. Rather than representing only a breakdown in muscle function, the shift toward slow-twitch fibers appears to be a protective response.

When cardiolipin concentrations fall, damaged mitochondria produce much larger quantities of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These highly reactive molecules can harm cellular structures, but they also play an important role in signaling that something is wrong.

The researchers found that ROS help initiate the transition from fast-twitch to slow-twitch muscle fibers. When they treated muscle cells lacking cardiolipin with an antioxidant to reduce ROS, the transformation became less pronounced.

A protein known as ERRγ plays a central role in coordinating this response. It directs cells to reorganize their mitochondria and change their muscle fiber characteristics. When scientists inhibited ERRγ in muscle cells grown in the laboratory, the transition between fiber types stopped entirely.

The team also discovered how the newly remodeled fibers help defend themselves.

Mice with insufficient cardiolipin absorbed considerably more glucose from their bloodstreams. However, their muscles were not primarily using this additional sugar to produce energy.

Instead, experiments that tracked specially labeled glucose showed that muscle cells redirected the sugar toward manufacturing their own antioxidants. This helped protect them against the damaging effects of excess ROS.

"The fiber switch is not the muscle failing, but the muscle trading power for protection. That's also why interfering with it can backfire: when we gave the mice antioxidants to mop up the ROS, their muscles fared worse, not better," says Assistant Professor Fabian Finger, first and co-corresponding author, from the University of Copenhagen.

A Potential New Approach to Treating Muscle Wasting

Although the findings point toward possible treatments for age-related muscle decline, the experiments demonstrating the protective mechanism and reversal of muscle wasting were conducted in mice. Human muscle samples were used only to establish that cardiolipin levels also decrease with age in people.

Nevertheless, researchers already have some ways to influence cardiolipin.

The FDA recently granted accelerated approval to elamipretide, a medication designed to help stabilize cardiolipin, for Barth syndrome, a rare inherited disorder. This suggests that targeting the molecule is medically feasible, although its effectiveness against ordinary age-related muscle loss remains unknown.

Another potential treatment target is ERRγ, the protein responsible for helping muscles adapt to mitochondrial stress.

ERRγ belongs to a family of proteins called nuclear receptors. These proteins are already established targets for approximately 10 to 15 percent of FDA-approved medications made from small molecules. Drugs that activate ERRγ are also being investigated in preclinical research for other medical applications.

The findings suggest that future therapies might work by restoring cardiolipin levels or by influencing the protective adaptations controlled by ERRγ.

"What encourages me most is that even a partial recovery of cardiolipin was enough to bring the muscle back. The question now is whether we can increase cardiolipin in aging muscle or target ERRγ to promote healthy adaptations. This is where the therapeutic potential lies," says senior author Zachary Gerhart-Hines, Associate Professor at the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research, University of Copenhagen.

The research involved scientists from more than 20 institutions. It was led by the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research at the University of Copenhagen in collaboration with the Center for Adipocyte Signaling at the University of Southern Denmark.

Financial support came from the Novo Nordisk Foundation, European Research Council, Lundbeck Foundation, US National Institutes of Health, and additional funding organizations.

Materials provided by University of Copenhagen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5664. Rocket Beats Expectations in Q3 Earnings Report Amid Stressed Mortgage Market

Despite operating in “one of the hardest mortgage markets in a generation” that’s “punishing” for American families as described by its CEO, Rocket Companies reported Q3 adjusted earnings above Wall Street expectations, with shares rising about 3% in after-hours trading Oct. 29.

Rocket reported a GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles) total revenue of $3.28B, up 18% from Q2’s $2.78B in total revenue; and adjusted revenue of $2.57B, down almost 7% from Q2’s adjusted revenue of $2.76B, but a notable 200%-plus increase in net income of $709M this quarter from last quarter’s net income of $229M. Adjusted net income and adjusted EBITDA were both down slightly from last quarter to $419M and $748M, respectively.

But looking at Rocket’s year-over-year earnings shows a total top-line turnaround. Its GAAP total net revenue increased over 94% from $1.69B; adjusted revenue up 37% from $1.87B; adjusted net income up 165% from $158M; adjusted EBITDA up 114% from $349M and most notably, a net income increase from a $124M loss swinging to that $709M profit.

In a release, Rocket Companies CEO and Director Varun Krishna attributed the numbers coming in against a backdrop of mortgage rates at three-year highs, to gains in both purchase and refinance.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” said Krishna. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology. We changed the economics of our business. Rates went up. We took share. Profits grew. That’s not a coincidence.”

In an investor call following the release of the data, Krishna attributed Rocket’s turnaround to a company rebuild three years ago that’s “built for any cycle,” which today is experiencing historic housing market hardships—from the 10-year Treasury rising to its highest point in 24 years to mortgage rates rising to their highest point in three years, to declines in existing-home sales and refinance applications.

“Here’s the truth about tough markets: they don’t lie,” he said. “They strip everything down to what’s real—who has the capital to keep investing, whose model works in any cycle, who can win their clients back, and who can move fast when it counts. This quarter did all of this. This was our highest margin in nearly five years and our fourth straight quarter of expansion since we closed the Mr. Cooper transaction. Adjusted net income of $419 million; $0.15 of adjusted EPS.

“So why does Rocket win?” he continued. “It’s no accident. Three years ago we made a decision: Rebuild this company at every single level. An ecosystem that serves clients from home search through servicing. A technology platform built for scale, speed and efficiency. Distribution that reaches homebuyers and homeowners everywhere. And a fortress balance sheet, now over $11 billion in liquidity, so we can keep investing while others pull back.”

On the investor call, Rocket Companies’ Chief Financial Officer Brian Brown walked through the Q3 numbers in more detail.

“We expanded adjusted EBITDA margin to its highest level in nearly five years, and we ended the quarter with record liquidity,” he said, noting that the $2.6B adjusted revenue was near the midpoint of its guidance range (an estimate of the company’s future financial performance). He said the company generated $40.4 billion in net rate lock volume and $43.6 billion in closed loan volume and that based on its estimates, purchase market share approached 6.5% and refinance market share was 15.5%. That’s compared to the 6.2% and 14.3% reported in the second quarter, he added.

Brown also commented that Rocket Local, its team of in-market loan officers who work directly with real estate agents, also grew volume more than 30% year-over-year, and now includes 400 loan officers across several major metro areas. He said the company’s partnership with Redfin and Compass extends that reach, with one in five of its purchase clients represented by a Redfin or Compass agent.

On the wholesale and partner lending side, he said over the last few months, the company has added around 200 new Rocket Pro partners to its platform, representing $12 billion in potential annual volume. Refinance volume set a record, Brown noted, saying cash-out refinance volume remained healthy, supported by another step up in recapture.

“Recapture rates on the combined portfolio reached an all-time high, the fourth consecutive quarter of improvement. Gain on sale margin, excluding correspondent, was 333 basis points, up from 311 basis points last quarter,” he said.

Krishna said that more than 70% of the company’s revenue this year is coming from recurring or less rate-sensitive sources, such as servicing fees, subscriptions, purchase, cash-out refinance and home equity. He said because of the firm’s integration with Redfin, mortgage buyers are brought into their ecosystem early, creating a path to Rocket from the beginning of their home-search journey. He said as of this earnings report, visitors who click through to start a purchase mortgage transaction are up 50% year-over-year.

“Redfin’s contribution to our refinance leads also more than doubled this quarter from a year ago,” Krishna said. “Compass simply extends that same playbook and delivers what buyers want most—homes and the agents who sell them. Cumulative unique listings are now nearly 40,000, up from roughly 25,000 last quarter. Homes you cannot find anywhere else. Rocket Pro net rate lock volume through Compass has passed $3 billion since February, up 50% from last quarter. Then there’s servicing—our ballast. More than $1 billion a quarter in servicing fees. More than $4 billion a year. That’s triple where we were three years ago. That’s recurring cash flow in any rate environment, revenue that shows up whether rates are 4% or 8%. And here’s what makes it compound: Because we know these clients; we’re first in line when they’re ready for their next loan. In Q3, recapture across the combined portfolio hit the highest level in our history.”

Rocket has a three-year agreement with Compass to provide national exposure to its private and coming-soon listings via Redfin.

Krishna said advances in AI in mortgage lending are a game-changer for Rocket, citing four segments of the process: Credit pulls, digital refinance, voice agents and the future of agentic AI.

On nearly 20% of its direct-to-consumer volume, AI completed the credit pull step on digital purchase and refinance leads before the client spoke to a loan officer, he said.

On refinance loans, he said clients can choose to pull their credit, see their loan options and lock their rate without having to speak to a loan officer. In Q3, he said digital was more than 40% of all direct-to-consumer refinance applications, and digital leads converted at four times the rate of every other channel.

Rocket’s AI voice agents now handle 65% of inbound servicing calls and resolve more than half of them on their own, Krishna added. On the future of agentic AI, he said consumers are starting to shop with their own AI agents to compare price, speed and ratings across lenders. Over the past 18 months, Rocket has built the APIs and protocols those agents need to complete the mortgage process with Rocket end to end, he noted.

Looking ahead, Brown said he expects the economic headwinds that have hammered the better part of this year to continue in Q4 and beyond, especially in the refinance sector.

“The MBA Purchase Application Index is down nearly 20% year-over-year, and refinance applications are down more than 50%,” he said. “The fourth quarter is seasonally low for our industry, and this year that slowdown comes at a time where mortgage rates are reaching highs we haven’t seen in two decades.”

Brown added that Rocket expects the refinance market to decline by almost half from the third quarter, “which would leave the overall mortgage activity near multi-decade lows.”

With that context, in the fourth quarter, Brown said they expect adjusted revenue to be between $2.1B and $2.3B with their guidance reflecting continued share gains. For expenses, they expect total expenses of $2.05B, including $110M of intangible amortization, $80M of stock-based compensation and $10M of one-time integration costs. Excluding these items, Brown said they expect expenses of $1.85B, a decline of $165M from the third quarter.

“Tough markets drive separation,” Brown said in his closing remarks. “This quarter, rates rose, volumes fell, and the industry felt it. Rocket Companies grew share, expanded margin, delivered synergies ahead of plan and ended the quarter with record liquidity. The fourth quarter will be harder still. We’re ready for it.”

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5663. 5 Packing Tips for a Smooth Move

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

Her lawyers will also attempt to seek reduced charges as an alternative, meaning there could be a bench trial instead of jury trial.

Lindsay Clancy has returned to court—two months after the jurors serving in the highly-publicized trial revealed they were deadlocked, forcing the judge to declare a mistrial, after an intense five-week courtroom showdown, during which they heard testimony from dozens of witnesses—and even visited the Massachusetts house where the former nurse is accused of murdering her children.

While Judge Sullivan overruled Phippen's objection, he put certain restrictions in place for the visit, limiting it to jurors, attorneys, and any court staff that were deemed necessary. He also barred any jurors from opening any closets or touching any of Phippen's personal items.

Phippen—who served as an assistant DA from April 2016 until December 2018, according to his LinkedIn page—purchased the home from Clancy's husband in an off-market deal in January 2024, almost a year to the day after the killings took place.

Property records show that he paid $675,000 for the three-bedroom dwelling, despite the fact that it was estimated to be worth closer to $800,000 at the time.

After Clancy's trial began, social media users began speculating that Phippen was involved in her case in some way, because it was being handled by the same District Attorney's office that he once worked for.

However, Phippen had not worked as an assistant DA for six years by the time he bought the property and his LinkedIn page shows that he established his own legal office in December 2018—and also now works as an attorney for Stark | Lattuca.

Other than the objection that he filed during the pretrial hearing, Phippen is not thought to have had any involvement in Clancy's trial. He has also never publicly discussed how he came to purchase the home.

The former nurse's husband, Patrick, first revealed that he had sold the property in October 2024, when he took part in an interview with The New Yorker, telling the outlet that he had offloaded the residence and relocated to an apartment in New York in the wake of his children's deaths.

He and Clancy had purchased the property for $500,000 in 2018, according to records.

In the interview, Patrick insisted that he "wasn't married to a monster," explaining how his wife had been suffering from anxiety and insomnia, which were brought on by her pregnancy with Callan.

Weeks before the terrible tragedy, he said, she had been hospitalized before being sent home with anti-depressants. Despite all this, he said that he believed that her only diagnosis was a generalized anxiety disorder.

“I wasn’t married to a monster—I was married to someone who got sick,” he told the publication, adding that he had chosen to speak out to prevent further "lies and misinformation" from being spread.

Closing arguments in Clancy's trial took place on Aug. 27, with the former nurse's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, reemphasized his argument that his client was in a "state of psychosis" when her children were killed, insisting that she cannot be found guilty of murder because of a "lack of criminal responsibility."

"Please have confidence in what you're about to do, all right? I have that confidence in you," he said, according to NBC News. "I don't think I've ever seen a more dedicated group of jurors in any trial that I've ever been involved in."

#5658. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5657. Philadelphia Renters Win Record Settlement Over Unsafe Conditions and Illegal Rent Collection

A group of Philadelphia renters has reached a settlement in one of the largest per-tenant recovery class action suits in the city’s rental law history.

A preliminary approval of the settlement, which requires Odin Properties LLC to provide the tenants at Bentley Manor apartments with rent forgiveness and refunds for wrongly collected rent, was finalized by a Philadelphia judge last week.

The aggregate settlement amount exceeds $140,000, and individual renters will receive varying amounts based on their payment history, with the average refund estimated at about $1,200.

Three residents of Bentley Manor, located in West Oak Lane, filed a class action suit in March 2025 against Odin Properties and related companies for allegedly illegally collecting rent after the building was designated “unsafe” by the Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I), according to The Public Interest Law Center.

Philadelphia law prohibits a landlord from collecting rent if a serious L&I violation if not corrected within 30 days. However, the plaintiffs alleged that Odin Properties continued to charge, demand, and collect rent each month, even as the building remained in unsafe status.

Odin Properties will now be required to forgive all unpaid rent and associated fees, estimated to be $66,891, and provide $75,000 in cash refunds for any rent collected, for a total of $141,891 in relief.

“This case sends a simple message: Landlords cannot collect rent while ignoring serious safety violations,” Madison Gray, the staff attorney at the Public Interest Law Center, tells Realtor.com®. “We hope it becomes clear that collecting rent while ignoring serious safety violations is a losing business model in Philadelphia, and we hope it encourages every landlord in the city to fix dangerous conditions promptly and comply with the law before tenants are forced to go to court.”

Realtor.com reached out to Odin Properties for a statement, but received no response.

Bentley Manor, which has approximately 71 sets of renters, was constructed in 1962. Between November 2021 and February 2024, L&I issued several violations related to fire safety, electrical hazards, and nonlatching building doors, all of which were resolved, according to the complaint.

On Nov. 14, 2024, L&I issued another notice of violation declaring the building an “unsafe structure,” citing “loose and missing bricks” and a “leaning parapet” as dangerous conditions. At the same time, multiple previous violations continued to resurface.

When the class-action complaint was filed four months later, in March, Odin Properties had allegedly still not made the building safe to the satisfaction of L&I, which made it ineligible to collect rent.

“Nevertheless, the Odin Defendants charged and collected rent from Plaintiffs and other tenants in December 2024, and in January, February, and March, 2025,” the complaint reads.

Three tenants were named as plaintiffs in the complaint: SEPTA transit operator Porter Grant, who paid $1,274 in monthly rent; Philadelphia police officer Casey Allison, who paid $1,352 in monthly rent; and a grandmother with mobility impairments, Dawn Colbourne, who paid $317 in monthly rent with the Philadelphia Housing Authority paying a monthly $968 subsidy.

“Without admitting or conceding any wrongdoing, liability, or damages, the Defendants have agreed to settle the Action to avoid the substantial expense, inconvenience, burden, and disruption of continued litigation,” the settlement document reads.

In between the lawsuit being filed in March 2025 and the settlement, the defendants made the necessary repairs to Bentley Manor.

Tenants will receive individualized amounts of the $75,000 settlement pool based on how much they paid during the non-compliance time period. On average, tenants will receive more than $1,200 per refund check, according to Gray.

“We also hope this sends a message to tenants. Philadelphia's housing laws only matter if they're enforced, and they don't enforce themselves,” says Gray. “This settlement shows that when landlords break the rules, tenants can fight back and win. Ultimately, we hope this settlement shows that tenants can hold even large landlords accountable when those laws are broken.”
